intro.t: An orderly, carefully researched account of the Saviour of the world, with a special eye for the poor, women and outsiders.
b: Luke is the first volume of a two-part history; Acts is the second. He writes for ‘most excellent Theophilus’ so that he ‘may know the certainty’ of what he has been taught (1:4). His is the longest Gospel, and it alone gives us the births of John and Jesus in detail, the shepherds, the boy Jesus in the temple, and many of Jesus’ best-loved parables: the Good Samaritan, the lost son, the rich man and Lazarus, the Pharisee and the tax collector.

Luke shows Jesus as the Saviour of all: Gentiles as well as Jews, women as well as men, the poor, the sick, Samaritans, tax collectors and sinners. ‘For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost’ (19:10). He stresses prayer, the Holy Spirit and joy, and the central section (9:51–19:27) is a long journey to Jerusalem, where Jesus dies, rises and ascends.

Luke and Acts are two volumes by one author: both are dedicated to ‘Theophilus’, Acts calls itself the sequel to a ‘first book’ about all that Jesus did and taught (Acts 1:1), and the two share language and style. In parts of Acts the writer says ‘we’ (Acts 16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), indicating that he travelled with Paul.

The early church names him unanimously as Luke, the ‘beloved physician’ and companion of Paul (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11). The Muratorian Canon (about AD 170) says: ‘The third book of the Gospel is that according to Luke. Luke, the well-known physician…composed it in his own name.’ The oldest manuscript of the Gospel, P75 (about AD 175–225), has the title ‘The Gospel according to Luke’, and the anti-Marcionite prologue calls him ‘an Antiochene, Syrian by race, physician by trade’.

Most scholars accept that the author was a companion of Paul, and many that it was Luke. Some argue the ‘we’ passages come from a source the author used. Luke is the only Gentile writer of the New Testament, and his two books make up over a quarter of it.

b: Three dates are proposed: the early 60s, AD 70–90, and the early 2nd century. The Lexham Bible Dictionary calls the debate ‘inconclusive’. The main argument for an early date is that Acts, the sequel, ends with Paul still awaiting trial in Rome (about AD 62) and does not mention his death, Nero’s persecution or the fall of Jerusalem. The main argument for a later date is that Luke used Mark, often dated to the late 60s, and that Luke 21:20 (‘Jerusalem surrounded by armies’) may reflect the siege of AD 70. A 2nd-century date is a minority view.

b: Luke tells Theophilus that he has ‘carefully investigated everything from the beginning’ using eyewitness accounts (1:1–4). For much of the 19th and 20th centuries many scholars doubted his reliability. But later work on Roman law, classical history, archaeology and ancient sea travel, by scholars such as William Ramsay, A. N. Sherwin-White and F. F. Bruce, has repeatedly vindicated his accuracy in details.

One example is his use of official titles, which varied from place to place and changed over time: ‘Caesar Augustus’ (2:1), ‘tetrarch’ for Herod Antipas (3:1), ‘king’ for Herod the Great (1:5), and many more in Acts. The Lexham Bible Dictionary notes that none of his titles has been shown to be wrong. F. F. Bruce’s summary: ‘Accuracy is a habit of mind.’ See also the drop-downs on Lysanias (3:1) and the census (2:1).

hist.t: Matthew, Mark and Luke: who used whom? (the ‘Synoptic problem’)
b: Matthew, Mark and Luke tell many of the same stories, often in the same order and with the same wording; they are called the ‘Synoptic’ Gospels (Greek: ‘seen together’). Of Mark’s 661 verses, about 606 have a parallel in Matthew and about 380 in Luke; only some 31 verses of Mark have no parallel in either.

Mark first (Widely accepted). Since the 19th century most scholars have concluded that Mark was written first and that Matthew and Luke each used it, smoothing its rough Greek and adding their own material. The material Matthew and Luke share but Mark lacks (about 200–250 verses, mostly sayings of Jesus) is usually explained by a lost collection of sayings called ‘Q’ (from German Quelle, ‘source’). Some suggest Papias’s remark that Matthew compiled ‘the oracles’ refers to something like it.

Other views (Debated). Augustine thought Mark had abridged Matthew, and many Catholic scholars long defended Matthew’s priority; a minority still argue that Matthew came first, or that Luke used Matthew directly with no need for Q. No copy of Q has ever been found.

None of these theories requires that the Gospel writers were careless or untrustworthy. Luke openly says he used earlier accounts and eyewitness testimony (Luke 1:1–4). Using written sources was normal and responsible history-writing.

1.t: Luke states his method: eyewitnesses, careful investigation, orderly writing, so that Theophilus may have certainty. The only Gospel to open by explaining itself.
Mary's song is closer to a revolutionary manifesto than a lullaby — the proud scattered, rulers pulled down, the hungry filled. It draws heavily on Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2.

2.t: Luke fixes the birth in datable imperial history. The word often rendered 'inn' more likely means the guest room of a family house.
A disreputable trade, and the first to be told. Luke's interest in the overlooked starts here and never stops.

4.t: Jesus reads Isaiah 61, stops mid-sentence before the day of vengeance, and says it is fulfilled. The crowd turns when he points out that Elijah and Elisha were sent to Gentiles.

5.t: Peter's first reaction to a miracle is to ask Jesus to leave. Luke understands that proximity to holiness is uncomfortable before it is good news.

7.t: Two debtors, two responses, and the point that much forgiveness produces much love. Luke's parallel to this scene is the prodigal son.

10.t: Told to a lawyer trying to limit the definition of neighbour. Jesus reverses the question: not who qualifies, but who acts like one.
Not a rebuke of work but of anxiety. Mary has taken the posture of a disciple, which in that culture was not a woman's place.

15.t: Sheep, coin, son — each with rejoicing at the finding. The elder brother is the point of the third, and the parable is left unfinished because the audience is the elder brother.

16.t: The only parable in which Jesus names one of his own characters. Its sting is the last line: they would not be convinced even if someone rose from the dead.

18.t: The clearest picture of justification in the Gospels. One man lists his record and goes home unjustified; the other asks for mercy and does not.

19.t: Luke's summary of Jesus' mission — to seek and to save the lost — is given at the end of this story rather than the start of the book.

22.t: Jesus tells Peter he has prayed for him and that he will turn back — the failure is predicted and the restoration promised in the same breath.

23.h: Today you will be with me
23.t: Luke alone records the criminal on the cross. Nothing is offered except a request, and nothing is required except it.

24.t: Jesus explains himself from Moses and all the Prophets. The best statement in Scripture of how the Old Testament is to be read.
He eats fish to prove he is not a ghost. Luke insists on the physicality of the resurrection.

3.t: Luke fixes John's ministry against six named rulers. He is writing history and wants it checkable.
Where Matthew traces Jesus to Abraham, Luke goes to Adam and then to God. His Gospel is for everyone, not only for Israel.

6.t: Luke's version is blunter than Matthew's: blessed are you who are poor, and woe to you who are rich. He does not spiritualise it.
The hardest instruction in the Gospels, grounded not in results but in the character of the Father who is kind to the ungrateful.

8.t: Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna, and says they supported the work out of their own means. No other Gospel records this.
Two demonstrations of authority, over nature and over the demonic. The healed man is told to stay and tell, which is the opposite of the usual instruction.

9.h: Who do you say I am
9.t: Luke places Peter's confession after a note that Jesus was praying alone. The call to take up the cross follows immediately, with Luke's addition: daily.
The turn of the Gospel. From here everything moves toward Jerusalem, and when a Samaritan village refuses him, he rebukes the disciples rather than the village.

11.t: Luke's shorter form of the Lord's Prayer, followed by the friend at midnight and the promise that the Father gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask. Persistence is commended, not because God is reluctant but because we are.
Luke's version of the denunciations, delivered over dinner at a Pharisee's house. The charge against the lawyers is that they took away the key of knowledge.

12.t: A man with a good harvest and no thought beyond himself. God's verdict lands on the one thing he had not planned for.
The ravens and the lilies again, ending with the instruction to sell possessions and give — Luke is consistently more concrete about money than Matthew.

13.t: Two disasters, and Jesus refuses the assumption that the victims were worse sinners. He turns the question back on the askers.
Asked whether few will be saved, Jesus does not answer the arithmetic. He tells them to strive to enter.

14.t: Table etiquette as kingdom instruction, ending with the advice to invite those who cannot repay.
The tower builder and the king going to war. Jesus is actively thinning a crowd here, which is worth noticing.

17.t: Ten lepers healed, one returns, and he is a Samaritan. Luke's interest in the outsider surfaces again.
Not coming with observable signs. The phrase can be rendered 'within you' or 'among you'; the second fits the context, since he is speaking to Pharisees.

20.t: As in Matthew and Mark. Luke notes the people's reaction — may it never be — which shows they understood.
Jesus poses the puzzle from Psalm 110 and leaves it hanging. The answer is the incarnation.

21.t: Luke places this immediately before the temple's destruction is predicted, as Mark does. She gives everything to something about to fall.
Luke's version is more explicit than Mark's about armies surrounding Jerusalem, which many take as evidence of how the AD 70 element was understood.

1.ctx: Ancient historians often opened with a formal preface like this one, and dedicated their works to a patron. ‘Most excellent’ was a title for officials of high rank (compare Acts 23:26; 26:25).
1.mean: ‘Many have undertaken to compose an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us, just as they were handed down to us by the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word.’ Luke has ‘carefully investigated everything from the beginning’ and writes ‘an orderly account’ for Theophilus, ‘so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught.’
1.big: Christian faith rests on events attested by eyewitnesses and carefully researched; it invites investigation.
1.diff: Inspiration and research. Luke used sources and did research, yet Christians confess his Gospel as inspired Scripture. All historic traditions hold these together: God worked through Luke’s ordinary methods. Calvin noted that Luke’s diligence does not lessen the Spirit’s guidance of his writing.

1.ctx: Priests were divided into twenty-four divisions (1 Chronicles 24; Abijah’s was the eighth), each serving in the temple for a week twice a year. With hundreds of priests, a man might be chosen to offer the incense only once in his life. Barrenness was often seen as a disgrace.
1.mean: Zechariah and Elizabeth are old, righteous and childless. Chosen by lot to burn incense in the temple, Zechariah sees the angel Gabriel: ‘Do not be afraid, Zechariah, because your prayer has been heard. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to give him the name John.’ He will be filled with the Holy Spirit from the womb, and ‘will go on before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah’, to ‘make ready a people prepared for the Lord.’ Zechariah asks for proof; for his unbelief he is struck silent until it happens. Elizabeth conceives: ‘The Lord has done this for me’.
1.big: After four hundred years of prophetic silence, God speaks again, in the temple, and the forerunner Malachi promised is on the way.

1.ctx: Nazareth was an obscure village in Galilee (see the drop-down at 4:16). Mary was betrothed, perhaps in her early teens, as was usual.
1.mean: Gabriel comes to ‘a virgin pledged in marriage to a man named Joseph’: ‘Greetings, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you.’ She will conceive a son and name him Jesus: ‘He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. The Lord God will give Him the throne of His father David, and He will reign over the house of Jacob forever. His kingdom will never end!’ ‘How can this be,’ Mary asked the angel, ‘since I am a virgin?’ ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. So the Holy One to be born will be called the Son of God.’ ‘For no word from God will ever fail.’ ‘I am the Lord’s servant,’ Mary answered. ‘May it happen to me according to your word.’
1.big: God’s eternal Son becomes human through the Spirit’s work in a virgin, the promised King of David’s line; and Mary responds with humble trust.
1.diff: ‘Highly favored’ (Greek kecharitōmenē; Latin tradition ‘full of grace’). Catholic teaching sees in this greeting a sign that Mary was ‘wholly borne by God’s grace’ and, through the centuries, came to the dogma of her Immaculate Conception (1854): that she ‘was redeemed from the moment of her conception’ (Catechism 490–491). The Orthodox honour Mary as all-holy but do not accept the Western dogma. Protestants read the word as God’s undeserved favour: Calvin said it ‘denotes the undeserved favor of God’, the same verb Paul uses of all believers in Ephesians 1:6; Wesley noted that ‘highly favoured’ is ‘no more than was said of Noah, Moses, and David’. All agree Mary is a model of faith and that her son, not she, is the Saviour.

1.ctx: The ‘hill country of Judah’ was about 100 km south of Nazareth, a journey of several days.
1.mean: Mary hurries to visit Elizabeth. At her greeting the baby leaps in Elizabeth’s womb, and Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, exclaims, ‘Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And why am I so honored, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?’ ‘Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord’s word to her will be fulfilled.’
1.big: Even before birth, John recognises Jesus; and Elizabeth calls Mary’s unborn child ‘my Lord’.
1.diff: ‘The mother of my Lord’. The Council of Ephesus (431) called Mary Theotokos, ‘God-bearer’ or ‘Mother of God’, to affirm that the child she bore was truly God, one person, not two; Catholic and Orthodox Christians use the title widely (Catechism 495). Calvin saw the same point in Elizabeth’s words: it ‘denotes a unity of person in the two natures of Christ’, so that the one born of Mary ‘is, at the same time, the eternal God’. Most Protestants accept the doctrine behind the title while preferring not to use it, lest it suggest Mary is the source of Christ’s divinity. Verses 28 and 42 form the first part of the Catholic ‘Hail Mary’ (Catechism 2676–2677). The unborn. Many Christians also see here the personhood of the unborn child.

1.ctx: The ‘Magnificat’ (from its first word in Latin) echoes Hannah’s song (1 Samuel 2:1–10) and many psalms. It is sung daily at Evening Prayer in many churches.
1.mean: ‘My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior! For He has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant. From now on all generations will call me blessed.’ ‘Holy is His name.’ Then she praises God’s great reversal: ‘He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty.’ God has helped Israel, remembering his promise to Abraham.
1.big: God lifts up the humble and brings down the proud; Mary rejoices in God as her Saviour.
1.diff: ‘All generations will call me blessed’. The Catholic Catechism opens its section on devotion to Mary with these words (971). Calvin stressed that Mary ‘makes her happiness to consist in nothing else, but in what she acknowledges to have been bestowed upon her by God’. Protestants also call her blessed, while declining prayer to her. ‘God my Savior’: Protestants see here Mary’s own need of a Saviour; Catholic teaching agrees she was saved by Christ, but holds that she was preserved from sin in advance by his merits (Catechism 491).

1.h: The Birth of John the Baptist
1.ctx: Boys were circumcised and named on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12). Children were usually named after relatives.
1.mean: Elizabeth gives birth, and her neighbours rejoice. On the eighth day they want to name the boy after his father. ‘No! He shall be called John.’ Zechariah writes, ‘His name is John.’ ‘Immediately Zechariah’s mouth was opened and his tongue was released, and he began to speak, praising God.’ People ask, ‘What then will this child become?’
1.big: Faith restored brings speech restored, and Zechariah’s first words are praise.

1.ctx: The ‘Benedictus’ (Latin for its first word) is sung daily at Morning Prayer in many churches. A ‘horn’ was a symbol of strength.
1.mean: Filled with the Spirit, Zechariah prophesies: ‘Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, because He has visited and redeemed His people. He has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David’, as promised to Abraham. Then to his son: ‘And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High; for you will go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him, to give to His people the knowledge of salvation through the forgiveness of their sins, because of the tender mercy of our God, by which the Dawn will visit us from on high’. John grows up in the wilderness.
1.big: God keeps his ancient promises: salvation comes through forgiveness, by his tender mercy, like the sunrise.

2.ctx: Augustus ruled the Roman Empire from 27 BC to AD 14 and was hailed as saviour and bringer of peace. Bethlehem, ‘house of bread’, was David’s town about 9 km south of Jerusalem. The word translated ‘inn’ (kataluma) is the word Luke uses for the ‘guest room’ of the Last Supper (22:11).
2.mean: ‘Now in those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that a census should be taken of the whole empire. This was the first census to take place while Quirinius was governor of Syria.’ Joseph, of David’s line, goes from Nazareth to Bethlehem to register, with Mary, who is pregnant. There ‘she gave birth to her firstborn, a Son. She wrapped Him in swaddling cloths and laid Him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.’
2.big: The Saviour of the world is born in obscurity, under the rule of a pagan emperor whose decree God used to bring Jesus to David’s town.
2.diff: Stable or guest room? Because Luke’s word for ‘inn’ is the same as ‘guest room’ in 22:11, some scholars suggest Joseph and Mary stayed in a relative’s crowded house, where animals were often kept in the lower part, and laid Jesus in a feeding trough there. Wesley suggested they were lodged ‘in the ox stall’. The traditional stable is not in the text, but the humble circumstances are.

b: The problem. Quirinius is well known from Roman sources. He was governor (legate) of Syria from AD 6 to 9, and held a census of Judea in AD 6 when Archelaus was deposed and Judea became a Roman province; Josephus records it, and so does Acts 5:37. But Jesus was born before Herod the Great died in 4 BC, so the census of Luke 2 must be at least nine years earlier. No other source mentions an empire-wide census at that time. Many scholars conclude that Luke confused the birth with the later census; one suggestion is that he confused Quirinius with Quinctilius Varus, governor of Syria at Herod’s death.

The case for Luke. F. F. Bruce, a classical scholar before he was a biblical one, notes that it is ‘widely agreed’ that such a census could have taken place in Judea near the end of Herod’s reign, when Augustus was treating Herod as a subject; that it could have been part of the empire-wide policy Luke describes, since there is evidence of census activity across the empire between 11 and 8 BC, including a regular series of censuses in Egypt every fourteen years from 10–9 BC; and that people returning to their family home to register, as Luke 2:3 describes, is attested in Egypt in AD 104.

On Quirinius himself, several solutions have been proposed. (1) He may have held an earlier command in Syria: an inscription found near Tivoli (the Lapis Tiburtinus) records an unnamed official who governed Syria ‘for the second time’, and William Ramsay identified him with Quirinius; Ronald Syme argued the earlier post was in Galatia instead. (2) Tertullian (about AD 207) says the census of Jesus’ birth was held under Sentius Saturninus, governor 8–6 BC. (3) The Greek of 2:2 can be translated ‘This census was before the one when Quirinius was governor of Syria’ (BSB footnote: ‘This was the census before’), so Luke may be distinguishing this census from the famous later one.

John Thorley, a classicist, points out that Luke is usually careful about political details and that before doubting him we should be sure we understand what he is saying; he concludes ‘The case must remain open.’ Given Luke’s proven accuracy elsewhere (see the drop-down on Lysanias at 3:1), many conservative scholars believe one of these solutions, or one not yet known, is right.

b: The emperor Constantine built a church over a cave in Bethlehem in the 4th century, at the place local Christians already honoured as Jesus’ birthplace; the present church is a later rebuilding. Justin Martyr, writing in the mid-2nd century, already says that Joseph, finding no lodging in Bethlehem, ‘took up his quarters in a certain cave near the village’. The New Bible Dictionary notes that Hadrian expelled Jews from Bethlehem in the 2nd century, so the site’s memory may have been interrupted, and the church ‘may or may not mark the true site’.

2.ctx: Shepherds worked outdoors with their flocks and were ordinary working men. David had been a shepherd of Bethlehem, and God is Israel’s shepherd (Psalm 23).
2.mean: An angel appears to shepherds at night: ‘Do not be afraid! For behold, I bring you good news of great joy that will be for all the people: Today in the city of David a Savior has been born to you. He is Christ the Lord!’ The sign: a baby in a manger. A great multitude of angels praise God: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men on whom His favor rests!’ The shepherds hurry and find the baby, spread the news, and return praising God. ‘But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart.’
2.big: The good news of the true Saviour and Lord is announced first to ordinary, despised people.
2.diff: ‘On earth peace to men on whom His favor rests’. Later manuscripts read ‘goodwill toward men’ (KJV). The better-attested reading means peace for those who receive God’s favour, that is, his grace, not those who show goodwill.

2.ctx: The Law required a mother to be purified forty days after a son’s birth with a lamb and a bird, or two birds if she was poor (Leviticus 12:8), and firstborn sons to be ‘consecrated’ to God (Exodus 13:2).
2.mean: On the eighth day Jesus is circumcised and named. When the time of purification is complete, Mary and Joseph bring him to the temple to present him to the Lord and offer ‘A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons’, the offering of the poor.
2.big: Jesus was born under the Law, into a poor family that faithfully kept it.

2.ctx: ‘The consolation of Israel’ was the promised comfort of Isaiah 40. Simeon’s song, the ‘Nunc Dimittis’, is sung at Evening Prayer and Compline.
2.mean: Simeon, righteous and devout, had been promised by the Spirit that he would see ‘the Lord’s Christ’ before he died. He takes the baby in his arms: ‘Sovereign Lord, as You have promised, You now dismiss Your servant in peace. For my eyes have seen Your salvation, which You have prepared in the sight of all people, a light for revelation to the Gentiles, and for glory to Your people Israel.’ To Mary he says the child will cause ‘the rise and fall of many in Israel’ and be opposed, ‘and a sword will pierce your soul as well.’
2.big: Jesus is God’s salvation for Gentiles and Israel alike; he will divide people, and his mother will share his suffering.

2.ctx: Asher was one of the northern tribes; some families kept their tribal identity after the exile.
2.mean: Anna, an aged prophetess, widowed after seven years of marriage, never left the temple, worshipping ‘night and day, fasting and praying.’ She gives thanks and speaks about the child ‘to all who were waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem.’
2.big: Faithful waiting is rewarded; an old woman becomes one of the first to tell others about Jesus.

2.ctx: Luke does not mention the flight to Egypt (Matthew 2:13–23); each Gospel selects its material.
2.mean: Having done all the Law required, they return to Nazareth. ‘And the Child grew and became strong. He was filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon Him.’
2.big: Jesus grew up normally in an ordinary town, under God’s grace.

2.h: The Boy Jesus at the Temple
2.ctx: At thirteen a Jewish boy became responsible for keeping the Law. Pilgrims travelled in large groups of relatives and neighbours.
2.mean: At twelve, Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem after Passover. After three days his parents find him in the temple, ‘sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions’. ‘Child, why have You done this to us?’ ‘Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You.’ ‘Why were you looking for Me?’ He asked. ‘Did you not know that I had to be in My Father’s house?’ They do not understand. He goes home and is obedient to them. ‘And Jesus grew in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and man.’
2.big: Even as a boy Jesus knew his unique relationship to the Father, yet he grew up as a real, obedient human child.
2.diff: How could the Son of God ‘grow in wisdom’? The church has confessed that Christ is truly God and truly man, ‘perfect in Godhead and also perfect in manhood’ (Chalcedon, 451). His human mind really learned and grew. Wesley: Jesus grew ‘As to his human nature’. See also the note on Mark 13:32.

3.h: The Mission of John the Baptist
3.ctx: Luke dates John’s ministry like a Greek historian. Tiberius succeeded Augustus in AD 14, so his fifteenth year is about AD 28–29. Annas had been high priest AD 6–15 and remained powerful; his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office.
3.mean: ‘In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea’, with Herod, Philip and Lysanias as tetrarchs, ‘during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John son of Zechariah in the wilderness.’ He preaches ‘a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins’, so that ‘all humanity will see God’s salvation.’ When the crowds ask, ‘What then should we do?’, he answers practically: share your clothes and food; tax collectors, ‘Collect no more than you are authorized’; soldiers, ‘Do not take money by force or false accusation’, ‘Be content with your wages.’ The coming one will baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire. Herod imprisons John for rebuking him.
3.big: Real repentance changes how we treat others, especially with money and power.

b: The only Lysanias named by ancient historians was a king executed by Mark Antony about 36 BC, some sixty years earlier, which made Luke’s reference look like an error. But an inscription from Abila, the capital of Abilene, dated between AD 14 and 29, records a temple dedication by a freedman of ‘Lysanias the tetrarch’. Josephus also speaks of Abila ‘which had been the tetrarchy of Lysanias’. Another inscription names two members of the family called Lysanias, of different generations. Luke’s Lysanias, tetrarch about AD 27–28, was a later member of the same family.

3.ctx: Luke often mentions Jesus praying at key moments (5:16; 6:12; 9:18, 28; 22:41).
3.mean: When all the people were being baptised, Jesus was baptised too. ‘And as He was praying, heaven was opened, and the Holy Spirit descended on Him in a bodily form like a dove.’ A voice: ‘You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.’
3.big: Father, Son and Spirit are revealed together as Jesus begins his work, in prayer.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 3:13–17; Luke 3:21–23 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

3.ctx: Luke traces the line backwards from Jesus to Adam, unlike Matthew, who goes forwards from Abraham.
3.mean: ‘Jesus Himself was about thirty years old when He began His ministry. He was regarded as the son of Joseph’, and the list goes back through Nathan, David, Abraham and Noah to ‘Adam, the son of God.’
3.big: Jesus belongs not only to Israel but to the whole human race, descended from Adam; he is the new head of humanity.
3.diff: See the note on Matthew 1:1 for the differences between the two genealogies. Some think Luke’s list gives Mary’s line (Joseph being Heli’s son-in-law); others, both lists Joseph’s. ‘He was regarded as the son of Joseph’ shows Luke knows Joseph was not his biological father.

F. F. Bruce, ‘Genealogy of Jesus Christ’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)

4.ctx: See the note on Matthew 4:1. Luke gives the temptations in a different order, ending in Jerusalem, the city where his Gospel climaxes.
4.mean: ‘full of the Holy Spirit’, Jesus is led into the wilderness and tempted for forty days. Bread from a stone: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone.’ All the world’s kingdoms, ‘For it has been relinquished to me’, if Jesus will worship the devil: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only.’ The temple pinnacle: ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test.’ ‘When the devil had finished every temptation, he left Him until an opportune time.’
4.big: Jesus resists every temptation with Scripture; the devil retreats only for a while.

4.ctx: Luke stresses the Holy Spirit in Jesus’ ministry (4:1, 14, 18).
4.mean: ‘Jesus returned to Galilee in the power of the Spirit’, and teaches in the synagogues, praised by everyone.
4.big: Jesus’ ministry is carried out in the Spirit’s power.

4.ctx: In a synagogue service, a reading from the Law was followed by one from the Prophets; a visitor could be invited to read and teach. Isaiah 61 speaks of the anointed servant and the ‘year of the Lord’s favor’, echoing the Jubilee when debts were cancelled and slaves freed (Leviticus 25).
4.mean: In Nazareth’s synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah 61: ‘The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to release the oppressed, to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.’ He sits down: ‘Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing.’ At first they are impressed: ‘Isn’t this the son of Joseph?’ But when he reminds them that Elijah was sent to a widow in Sidon and Elisha healed Naaman the Syrian, Gentiles both, they are enraged and try to throw him off a cliff. ‘But Jesus passed through the crowd and went on His way.’
4.big: Jesus announces himself as the Spirit-anointed bringer of release foretold by Isaiah, for Gentiles as well as Israel; his own town rejects him.
4.diff: Jesus stops reading before Isaiah’s next words, ‘and the day of our God’s vengeance’ (Isaiah 61:2). Many interpreters see his first coming as the time of favour, with judgment still to come.

b: Nazareth was a small Jewish farming village on a ridge in Lower Galilee: current estimates suggest 200–500 people in Jesus’ day. No writer before the New Testament mentions it, not even Josephus, which fits a place of no importance (compare John 1:46). Excavations under the Church of the Annunciation found silos, cisterns, tombs and simple houses.

About 6 km away stood Sepphoris, which Herod Antipas rebuilt as his capital after 4 BC. The word translated ‘carpenter’ (Greek tektōn) means a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Building work at Sepphoris would have drawn craftsmen from the surrounding villages, and many scholars think Joseph and Jesus may have worked there, though the Gospels never mention it.

4.ctx: See the note on Mark 1:21. Luke, writing for readers outside Palestine, explains that Capernaum is ‘a town in Galilee’.
4.mean: In Capernaum the people are astonished ‘because His message had authority.’ A man with an unclean demon cries out, ‘I know who You are—the Holy One of God!’ Jesus rebukes it and it comes out ‘without harming him.’ ‘What is this message? With authority and power He commands the unclean spirits, and they come out!’
4.big: Jesus’ word has authority over evil.

b: Capernaum, on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, was a small fishing town on the road to Damascus, with a tax post (compare Mark 2:14). A Roman milestone was found near the synagogue. The white limestone synagogue visitors see today dates from the 4th or 5th century AD (about 10,000 coins were found beneath its floor), but it stands on the foundations of an earlier one, probably the synagogue of Jesus’ day (compare Luke 7:5).

Just south of it is an octagonal church built over the walls of an earlier house. The excavators believe this was Peter’s house (Mark 1:29), venerated by Christians from early times; Italian archaeologists report the name Peter among graffiti scratched on its walls. The identification is reasonable but cannot be proved.

src.l: ‘Capernaum’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Shanks and Cole)

4.ctx: Luke, the doctor, describes a ‘high fever’. See the note on Mark 1:29.
4.mean: Jesus stands over Simon’s mother-in-law ‘and rebuked the fever, and it left her.’ She gets up and serves them. At sunset he lays hands on each of the sick and heals them; demons come out shouting ‘You are the Son of God!’, but he silences them.
4.big: Jesus deals personally with each person who comes to him.

4.ctx: ‘Judea’ here probably means the whole land of the Jews, including Galilee (BSB footnote).
4.mean: The crowds try to keep him in Capernaum. ‘I must preach the good news of the kingdom of God to the other towns as well, because that is why I was sent.’
4.big: Jesus’ priority is preaching the kingdom to everyone.

5.ctx: Luke calls the Sea of Galilee ‘the Lake of Gennesaret’, the name of the plain on its north-west shore. Fishing was best at night; by day the fish went deep.
5.mean: Jesus teaches from Simon’s boat, then tells him: ‘Put out into deep water and let down your nets for a catch.’ ‘Master,’ Simon replied, ‘we have worked hard all night without catching anything. But because You say so, I will let down the nets.’ The catch is so great the nets tear and two boats begin to sink. Peter falls at Jesus’ knees: ‘Go away from me, Lord,’ he said, ‘for I am a sinful man.’ ‘Do not be afraid,’ Jesus said to Simon. ‘From now on you will catch men.’ They leave everything and follow him.
5.big: Meeting Jesus’ power reveals our sin; but instead of sending sinners away, he calls them to follow and gives them a new purpose.

5.ctx: See the note on Mark 1:40. Luke the doctor says the man was ‘covered with leprosy’.
5.mean: A man covered with leprosy begs: ‘Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.’ Jesus touches him: ‘I am willing,’ He said. ‘Be clean!’ Crowds grow, ‘Yet He frequently withdrew to the wilderness to pray.’
5.big: Jesus is willing to cleanse; and his public power was rooted in private prayer.

5.ctx: See the note on Mark 2:1. Luke mentions roof tiles, a detail familiar to Greek readers.
5.mean: Friends lower a paralysed man through the roof tiles. ‘Friend, your sins are forgiven.’ The scribes and Pharisees think, ‘Who is this man who speaks blasphemy? Who can forgive sins but God alone?’ To show ‘that the Son of Man has authority on the earth to forgive sins’, Jesus heals him. ‘We have seen remarkable things today.’
5.big: Jesus forgives sins, as only God can, and proves it.

5.mean: Levi ‘got up, left everything, and followed Him’, then hosts ‘a great banquet’ for tax collectors and others. Pharisees complain. ‘It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners, to repentance.’
5.big: Jesus calls sinners to repentance, and celebrates with them when they come.

5.mean: ‘Can you make the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them? But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.’
5.big: Jesus’ presence is a wedding feast.

5.ctx: Only Luke adds the saying about old wine (verse 39).
5.mean: A patch torn from a new garment ruins both. New wine needs new wineskins. ‘And no one after drinking old wine wants new, for he says, ‘The old is better.’’
5.big: The new life Jesus brings needs new forms, and people comfortable with the old often do not want it.

6.mean: The disciples pick and rub grain on the Sabbath. Jesus cites David eating the consecrated bread. ‘The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath.’
6.big: Jesus is Lord of God’s holy day.

6.ctx: See the note on Mark 3:1. Luke the doctor notes it was the man’s right hand.
6.mean: ‘which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?’ He heals the withered hand; the scribes and Pharisees are ‘filled with rage’.
6.big: Doing good is always lawful on God’s day.

6.ctx: Luke’s list has ‘Judas son of James’ where Matthew and Mark have Thaddaeus, probably the same man with two names.
6.mean: Jesus ‘spent the night in prayer to God’, then chooses twelve ‘whom He also designated as apostles’, ending with ‘Judas Iscariot, who became a traitor.’
6.big: Jesus chose his apostles after a night of prayer.

6.ctx: Luke’s sermon is given ‘on a level place’; it is shorter than Matthew’s Sermon on the Mount and has much in common with it.
6.mean: A great crowd from Judea, Jerusalem and the coast of Tyre and Sidon come to hear him and be healed. ‘The entire crowd was trying to touch Him, because power was coming from Him and healing them all.’
6.big: Jesus’ power to heal flowed out to all who came.

6.ctx: Luke’s beatitudes speak directly (‘you’) and are about outward conditions; Matthew’s include ‘poor in spirit’ and ‘hunger and thirst for righteousness’.
6.mean: ‘Blessed are you who are poor, for yours is the kingdom of God. Blessed are you who hunger now, for you will be filled. Blessed are you who weep now, for you will laugh.’ Blessed when hated and excluded ‘because of the Son of Man’: ‘Rejoice in that day and leap for joy, because great is your reward in heaven.’
6.big: God’s blessing rests on the poor and suffering who belong to Jesus; their reversal is coming.
6.diff: Some see Luke’s version as more ‘social’ and Matthew’s as more ‘spiritual’. Most interpreters think both describe the same people: the poor and oppressed of God’s people who look to him, as in the Psalms, where ‘the poor’ are often the faithful afflicted.

6.ctx: Found only in Luke; the mirror image of the blessings.
6.mean: ‘But woe to you who are rich, for you have already received your comfort. Woe to you who are well fed now, for you will hunger. Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep. Woe to you when all men speak well of you’.
6.big: Comfort and popularity now can be the only reward a person gets.

6.ctx: See the notes on Matthew 5:38–48, including the different Christian views on non-resistance.
6.mean: ‘Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you.’ Turn the other cheek; give to all who ask. ‘Do to others as you would have them do to you.’ Even sinners love those who love them. ‘But love your enemies, do good to them, and lend to them, expecting nothing in return.’ ‘for He is kind to the ungrateful and wicked. Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful.’
6.big: Disciples imitate the mercy of their Father, who is kind even to the ungrateful.

6.ctx: Grain was measured into a fold of a garment (‘lap’), pressed down and shaken to fit more.
6.mean: ‘Do not judge, and you will not be judged. Do not condemn, and you will not be condemned. Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Give, and it will be given to you. A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over will be poured into your lap.’ A blind man cannot lead the blind; deal with the beam in your own eye first.
6.big: Generosity and mercy come back to us overflowing; harsh judgment comes back too.

6.mean: A tree is known by its fruit. ‘The good man brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart’. ‘For out of the overflow of the heart the mouth speaks.’
6.big: What we say and do shows what our hearts are.

6.mean: ‘Why do you call Me ‘Lord, Lord,’ but do not do what I say?’ The one who hears and acts is like a man who ‘dug down deep and laid his foundation on the rock’; the flood cannot shake his house. The one who does not act built without a foundation, ‘and great was its destruction!’
6.big: Calling Jesus Lord means doing what he says.

7.ctx: See the note on Matthew 8:5. Luke adds that the centurion sent Jewish elders and friends rather than coming himself.
7.mean: The elders plead: ‘This man is worthy to have You grant this, for he loves our nation and has built our synagogue.’ But the centurion sends word: ‘Lord, do not trouble Yourself, for I am not worthy to have You come under my roof.’ ‘But just say the word, and my servant will be healed.’ Jesus marvels: ‘I tell you, not even in Israel have I found such great faith.’ The servant is found well.
7.big: Others called him worthy; he knew he was not, and trusted Jesus’ word alone.
7.diff: Matthew says the centurion came to Jesus; Luke that he sent messengers. Interpreters commonly note that what a person does through agents is often said to be done by him, as Luke himself says the centurion ‘has built our synagogue’.

b: Capernaum, on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, was a small fishing town on the road to Damascus, with a tax post (compare Mark 2:14). A Roman milestone was found near the synagogue. The white limestone synagogue visitors see today dates from the 4th or 5th century AD (about 10,000 coins were found beneath its floor), but it stands on the foundations of an earlier one, probably the synagogue of Jesus’ day (compare Luke 7:5).

Just south of it is an octagonal church built over the walls of an earlier house. The excavators believe this was Peter’s house (Mark 1:29), venerated by Christians from early times; Italian archaeologists report the name Peter among graffiti scratched on its walls. The identification is reasonable but cannot be proved.

7.ctx: Nain was a village about 10 km south-east of Nazareth. A widow who lost her only son lost her means of support and her future. Elijah had raised a widow’s son (1 Kings 17:17–24).
7.mean: At the town gate Jesus meets a funeral: ‘the only son of his mother, and she was a widow.’ ‘When the Lord saw her, He had compassion on her and said, “Do not weep.”’ He touches the bier: ‘Young man,’ He said, ‘I tell you, get up!’ The dead man sits up and speaks, ‘Then Jesus gave him back to his mother.’ ‘A great prophet has appeared among us!’ ‘God has visited His people!’
7.big: Jesus’ compassion moves him to act, and his word overpowers death.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 7:11–17 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

7.mean: John sends two disciples: ‘Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?’ Jesus heals many in front of them, then says, ‘Go back and report to John what you have seen and heard’: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the dead are raised, ‘and the good news is preached to the poor.’
7.big: Jesus answers honest doubt with evidence that he fulfils Scripture.

7.ctx: See the note on Matthew 11:7. Only Luke records verses 29–30.
7.mean: John is a prophet and more, the promised messenger; yet the least in the kingdom is greater. ‘All the people who heard this, even the tax collectors, acknowledged God’s justice. For they had received the baptism of John. But the Pharisees and experts in the law rejected God’s purpose for themselves’. This generation complained about John’s fasting and Jesus’ feasting. ‘But wisdom is vindicated by all her children.’
7.big: Ordinary sinners accepted God’s purpose; the religious experts refused it.
7.diff: ‘Rejected God’s purpose for themselves’ is often cited by Arminian (Wesleyan) Christians to show that God’s gracious intentions can be resisted: Wesley wrote that they ‘made void…the gracious design, of God toward them’. Reformed theology distinguishes God’s revealed will in the gospel invitation, which people can and do reject, from his decree, which cannot fail.

src.l: John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Luke 7

7.ctx: At a formal meal guests reclined on couches, feet away from the table, and uninvited people could come in and watch. A host would normally offer water for the feet, a kiss of greeting and oil. A woman letting down her hair in public was shocking. This is a different event from the anointing at Bethany in Mark 14.
7.mean: A woman known as a sinner comes to the Pharisee’s house, weeps over Jesus’ feet, wipes them with her hair, kisses them and anoints them with perfume. Simon thinks, ‘If this man were a prophet, He would know who this is and what kind of woman is touching Him’. Jesus tells of two debtors forgiven, one 500 denarii and one 50: ‘Which one, then, will love him more?’ Simon gave Jesus no water, no kiss, no oil; she has given tears, kisses and perfume. ‘Therefore I tell you, her many sins have been forgiven, for she has loved much. But he who has been forgiven little loves little.’ ‘Your sins are forgiven.’ ‘Your faith has saved you; go in peace.’
7.big: Those who know how much they have been forgiven love much; and it is faith that saves.
7.diff: Was she forgiven because she loved? The parable shows love following forgiveness (the debtor forgiven more loves more), and Jesus ends ‘Your faith has saved you’. Most Protestant interpreters therefore read verse 47 as ‘her sins have been forgiven, as her great love shows’; Wesley: her love is ‘the effect and evidence, not the cause of her pardon’, ‘Not thy love’ but faith saved her. Catholic interpreters also hold that forgiveness is God’s free gift, while stressing love as part of the response of faith. Was she Mary Magdalene? Luke does not name her. In 591 Pope Gregory the Great identified her with Mary Magdalene and Mary of Bethany, and the idea that Mary Magdalene was a reformed prostitute became widespread in Western tradition. There is no evidence for it; Luke introduces Mary Magdalene in the next chapter as someone freed from seven demons.

John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Luke 7

8.ctx: Rabbis did not normally have women disciples travelling with them. Chuza managed the household or estates of Herod Antipas, so Joanna was a woman of some standing.
8.mean: Jesus travels preaching the kingdom with the Twelve ‘as well as some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, Joanna the wife of Herod’s household manager Chuza, Susanna, and many others. These women were ministering to them out of their own means.’
8.big: Women were among Jesus’ travelling followers and financial supporters, and they would be the first witnesses of the resurrection (24:10).

b: Mary Magdalene probably came from Magdala, a fishing town on the west shore of the Sea of Galilee, north of Tiberias, possibly the ‘Migdal Nunnaya’ (‘tower of fish’) of later Jewish texts. Recent excavations have uncovered a 1st-century synagogue there, and inside it a stone table carved with a relief of the Jerusalem temple. The Gospels do not say Jesus visited Magdala, but he taught in ‘their synagogues’ throughout Galilee (Mark 1:39), and this is the kind of building he would have known.

8.mean: A farmer sows seed on the path, rock, thorns and good soil. ‘The seed is the word of God.’ The devil takes it from some ‘so that they may not believe and be saved.’ Others ‘believe for a season, but in the time of testing, they fall away.’ Some are choked ‘by the worries, riches, and pleasures of this life’. ‘But the seeds on good soil are those with a noble and good heart, who hear the word, cling to it, and by persevering produce a crop.’
8.big: Hearing the word must lead to holding on to it and persevering.
8.diff: Luke’s ‘believe for a season’ sharpens the question discussed at Mark 4:13: Arminian readers see genuine but temporary faith; Reformed readers see a faith that was never rooted. Both take the call to persevere seriously.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 8:4–10 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

8.mean: Lamps are put on stands. Everything hidden will be revealed. ‘Pay attention, therefore, to how you listen. Whoever has will be given more, but whoever does not have, even what he thinks he has will be taken away from him.’
8.big: How we listen to God’s word matters.

8.ctx: See the notes on Mark 3:31 and 6:1.
8.mean: His mother and brothers cannot reach him for the crowd. ‘My mother and brothers are those who hear the word of God and carry it out.’
8.big: Hearing and doing God’s word makes us Jesus’ family.

8.mean: A windstorm swamps the boat while Jesus sleeps. ‘Master, Master, we are perishing!’ He rebukes wind and waves; all is calm. ‘Where is your faith?’ ‘Who is this? He commands even the winds and the water, and they obey Him!’
8.big: The Lord of nature is with his people in the storm.

8.ctx: See the note and drop-down on the location at Mark 5:1. ‘The Abyss’ was the place of imprisonment for evil spirits (Revelation 20:1–3).
8.mean: A naked man possessed by many demons (‘Legion’) lives among the tombs. The demons beg not to be sent ‘into the Abyss’ and go into the pigs, which drown. The people find the man ‘sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind’, and ask Jesus to leave. He sends the man home: ‘Return home and describe how much God has done for you.’ He tells everyone ‘how much Jesus had done for him.’
8.big: What God has done, Jesus has done; the freed man becomes his witness.

src.l: ‘Gerasenes’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

8.ctx: See the note on Mark 5:21. Some manuscripts lack Luke’s remark about the doctors (BSB footnote).
8.mean: Jairus’s only daughter, about twelve, is dying. A woman bleeding for twelve years touches Jesus’ cloak and is healed. ‘Someone touched Me, for I know that power has gone out from Me.’ ‘Daughter,’ said Jesus, ‘your faith has healed you. Go in peace.’ News comes that the girl is dead. ‘Do not be afraid; just believe, and she will be healed.’ ‘Child, get up!’ ‘Her spirit returned, and at once she got up.’
8.big: Jesus restores both the outcast woman and the dying child; faith in him is never too late.

9.mean: Jesus gives the Twelve ‘power and authority over all demons, and power to cure diseases’, and sends them to proclaim the kingdom and heal. ‘Take nothing for the journey’. They go ‘preaching the gospel and healing people everywhere.’
9.big: Jesus shares his mission with his followers.

9.ctx: Herod Antipas; see the drop-down at Mark 6:14. He would see Jesus at his trial (23:8).
9.mean: Herod is perplexed by reports about Jesus. ‘I beheaded John,’ Herod said, ‘but who is this man I hear such things about?’ ‘And he kept trying to see Jesus.’
9.big: Everyone has to answer the question ‘who is this?’

hist.t: Herod Antipas, Herodias and John’s death
b: The ‘King Herod’ of Mark 6 is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. After his father died in 4 BC, Augustus made him tetrarch (ruler of a quarter) of Galilee and Perea, which he governed for 43 years. Matthew and Luke give his exact title, ‘tetrarch’; Mark uses the popular ‘king’. He rebuilt Sepphoris and founded Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee.

Josephus confirms the outline of Mark’s account. Antipas divorced his first wife, daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, to marry Herodias, who had been married to his half-brother. Josephus calls that first husband Herod; Mark calls him Philip. Since several of Herod the Great’s sons were called Herod, some suggest he bore both names. Aretas later defeated Antipas in battle, and Josephus says many Jews saw the defeat as God’s punishment for his killing of ‘John, that was called the Baptist’, ‘a good man’ who called the Jews to righteousness and baptism.

Josephus gives a political reason for the execution: Antipas feared John’s influence over the crowds might lead to a revolt. Mark gives the personal story. The two fit together easily. Josephus says John was held and killed at Machaerus, Antipas’s fortress east of the Dead Sea.

9.h: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
9.ctx: See the note on Mark 6:30. Luke places it near Bethsaida (see the drop-down at Mark 8:22).
9.mean: Jesus welcomes the crowds, speaks of the kingdom and heals. ‘You give them something to eat.’ With five loaves and two fish he feeds five thousand men, seated in groups of fifty; twelve baskets are left.

src.l: ‘Bethsaida’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Arav)

9.ctx: See the notes on Mark 8:27 and Matthew 16:13. Luke notes Jesus was praying.
9.mean: After praying alone, Jesus asks, ‘Who do the crowds say I am?’ Then: ‘But what about you?’ Jesus asked. ‘Who do you say I am?’ Peter answered, ‘The Christ of God.’

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 9:18–20 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

9.mean: ‘The Son of Man must suffer many things’, be rejected, ‘and He must be killed and on the third day be raised to life.’
9.big: The Christ must suffer, die and rise.

9.mean: ‘If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.’ ‘What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet lose or forfeit his very self?’ Some standing there ‘will not taste death before they see the kingdom of God.’
9.big: Following Jesus is a daily dying to self.
9.diff: On ‘some who are standing here’, see the note on Mark 9:1.

9.ctx: See the note on Mark 9:1. Only Luke says what Moses and Elijah discussed: Jesus’ ‘departure’ (Greek exodos).
9.mean: On the mountain, ‘as He was praying, the appearance of His face changed, and His clothes became radiantly white.’ Moses and Elijah appear in glory ‘and spoke about His departure, which He was about to accomplish at Jerusalem.’ A cloud covers them: ‘This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!’
9.big: Jesus’ coming death in Jerusalem is a new exodus, the great act of deliverance the Law and the Prophets pointed to.

9.h: The Boy with an Evil Spirit
9.ctx: See the note on Mark 9:14. Luke notes the boy was an only child.
9.mean: A father begs, ‘look at my son, for he is my only child.’ The disciples could not help. ‘O unbelieving and perverse generation!’ Jesus rebukes the spirit, heals the boy ‘and gave him back to his father.’ ‘And they were all astonished at the greatness of God.’
9.big: Jesus restores what evil has taken.

9.h: The Second Prediction of the Passion
9.mean: ‘Let these words sink into your ears: The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men.’ ‘But they did not understand this statement. It was veiled from them’.
9.big: The cross was beyond the disciples’ understanding until after the resurrection (24:45).

9.mean: The disciples argue about who is greatest. Jesus stands a child beside him: ‘For whoever is the least among all of you, he is the greatest.’ Of an outsider casting out demons in his name: ‘Do not stop him’, ‘for whoever is not against you is for you.’
9.big: The least is the greatest in Jesus’ kingdom.

9.ctx: This begins Luke’s long travel section (9:51–19:27). Samaritans and Jews were bitter enemies; Samaritans worshipped on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem. Elijah had called fire down on soldiers (2 Kings 1:10–12).
9.mean: ‘As the day of His ascension approached, Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem.’ A Samaritan village refuses him because he is heading for Jerusalem. James and John ask, ‘Lord, do You want us to call down fire from heaven to consume them?’ Jesus rebukes them, and they go elsewhere.
9.big: Jesus sets his face towards the cross and refuses to call down judgment on those who reject him.
9.diff: Later manuscripts add Jesus’ words, ‘You do not know what kind of spirit you are of’ (BSB footnote; KJV). The earliest manuscripts lack them, though the meaning is the same.

b: The Samaritans lived in the hill country between Judea and Galilee. Jews regarded them as descendants of foreigners settled there by the Assyrians after 722 BC who had mixed with the remaining Israelites (2 Kings 17:24–41). The Samaritans saw themselves as the true descendants of the northern tribes. They accepted only the five books of Moses, and treated Mount Gerizim as their holy place; Josephus says they built a temple there, though this is debated. Hostility grew after the Jewish ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed their city of Shechem in 128 BC. A small Samaritan community, a few hundred strong, still exists in Israel today. Luke shows Jesus breaking through this hostility (10:25–37; 17:11–19).
