‘Samaritans’, New Bible Dictionary, 3rd ed. (IVP, 1996)
‘Samaritans’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

9.ctx: See the note on Matthew 8:18. When Elijah called Elisha, he allowed him to say goodbye to his family (1 Kings 19:19–21).
9.mean: ‘Foxes have dens and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head.’ ‘Let the dead bury their own dead. You, however, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.’ To one who wants to say farewell first: ‘No one who puts his hand to the plow and then looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.’
9.big: Following Jesus requires wholehearted commitment without looking back.

10.ctx: Some manuscripts say seventy (BSB footnote). Genesis 10 lists seventy nations (seventy-two in the Greek Old Testament), so the number may hint at the mission to all nations.
10.mean: Jesus sends seventy-two ahead of him in pairs: ‘The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few.’ ‘I am sending you out like lambs among wolves.’ They are to travel light, bless homes with peace, accept hospitality (‘the worker is worthy of his wages’), heal the sick and say, ‘The kingdom of God is near you.’ Towns that refuse them will fare worse than Sodom.
10.big: The mission is wider than the Twelve; ordinary followers are sent to announce the kingdom.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 10:1–12 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

10.mean: ‘Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida!’ Tyre and Sidon would have repented. Capernaum will be brought down to Hades. ‘Whoever listens to you listens to Me; whoever rejects you rejects Me; and whoever rejects Me rejects the One who sent Me.’
10.big: Rejecting Jesus’ messengers is rejecting Jesus and the Father.

10.ctx: Snakes and scorpions were common dangers and also symbols of evil powers.
10.mean: The seventy-two return rejoicing: ‘Lord, even the demons submit to us in Your name.’ ‘I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven.’ He has given them authority over ‘all the power of the enemy.’ ‘Nevertheless, do not rejoice that the spirits submit to you, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven.’
10.big: The defeat of Satan is under way; but the deepest joy is not spiritual power but belonging to God.
10.diff: ‘Your names are written in heaven’ (compare Exodus 32:32; Revelation 20:12). Reformed readers see here God’s eternal election as the ground of assurance; Arminian readers note that names can be ‘blotted out’ (Revelation 3:5 is often read as warning of this). Both agree that a disciple’s security rests on God’s grace, not on visible success.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 10:17–20 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

10.ctx: See the note on Matthew 11:25. Luke says Jesus ‘rejoiced in the Holy Spirit’.
10.mean: ‘I praise You, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because You have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children.’ ‘No one knows who the Son is except the Father, and no one knows who the Father is except the Son and those to whom the Son chooses to reveal Him.’ ‘Blessed are the eyes that see what you see.’
10.big: Knowing God is a gift revealed by the Son to the humble.
10.diff: See the note on Matthew 11:25 for Reformed and Wesleyan readings.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 10:21–22 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

10.h: The Parable of the Good Samaritan
10.ctx: The road from Jerusalem down to Jericho drops about 1,000 m through barren, rocky country in under 30 km. Priests and Levites served in the temple; touching a dead body would make them unclean. Jews and Samaritans despised each other (see the drop-down at 9:51).
10.mean: An expert in the law asks, ‘Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?’ He answers his own question with the two great commandments. ‘You have answered correctly,’ ‘Do this and you will live.’ ‘But wanting to justify himself, he asked Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?”’ Jesus tells of a man beaten and left half dead. A priest and a Levite pass by on the other side. ‘But a Samaritan on a journey came upon him, and when he saw him, he had compassion.’ He bandages him, takes him to an inn and pays for his care. ‘Which of these three do you think was a neighbor’? ‘The one who showed him mercy’. ‘Go and do likewise.’
10.big: The question is not ‘who qualifies as my neighbour?’ but ‘will I be a neighbour?’, even to an enemy.
10.diff: ‘Do this and you will live’. Is Jesus teaching salvation by works? Protestant interpreters, especially Lutheran and Reformed, read it as the law’s true demand, which no one perfectly keeps, so it drives us to grace (the lawyer’s wish ‘to justify himself’ shows the danger). Others stress that true faith expresses itself in this kind of love. Allegory? An old allegorical reading makes the Samaritan Christ rescuing wounded humanity. It can be a moving application, but Calvin warned against building doctrine on such allegories: one version, which used the ‘half dead’ man to argue that fallen people keep a free will, he called ‘too absurd to deserve refutation’. On ‘Do this and you will live’ Calvin says the law truly shows the way of righteousness, but ‘the fault lies not in the doctrine of the Law, but in men’. Jesus’ own application is simple: ‘Go and do likewise.’

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 10:25–37 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
‘Samaritans’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

10.ctx: Their village was Bethany, near Jerusalem (John 11:1). Sitting at a teacher’s feet was the posture of a disciple, unusual for a woman then.
10.mean: Martha welcomes Jesus and is ‘distracted by all the preparations’; her sister Mary ‘sat at the Lord’s feet listening to His message.’ Martha complains: ‘Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone? Tell her to help me!’ ‘Martha, Martha,’ the Lord replied, ‘you are worried and upset about many things. But only one thing is necessary. Mary has chosen the good portion, and it will not be taken away from her.’
10.big: Listening to Jesus is the one necessary thing; even service for him can crowd it out.
10.diff: This story was long used to rank the contemplative life (monks and nuns) above the active life. Calvin rejected praising withdrawal from work as ‘an Angelical life’, insisting that ‘no sacrifice is more pleasing to God, than when every man applies diligently to his own calling’. Most readers today see the point as priorities within every Christian life: hearing Christ comes first, and service flows from it.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 10:38–42 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

11.ctx: Luke’s version is shorter than Matthew’s (6:9–13); later copyists made Luke’s match Matthew’s (BSB footnotes). Jesus probably taught it more than once.
11.mean: A disciple asks, ‘Lord, teach us to pray, just as John taught his disciples.’ ‘When you pray, say: ‘Father, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come. Give us each day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins, for we also forgive everyone who sins against us. And lead us not into temptation.’’
11.big: Jesus teaches us to pray to God as ‘Father’, putting his name and kingdom first.

11.ctx: Hospitality to a traveller was a sacred duty. A family slept together on mats in a one-room house; getting up would wake everyone.
11.mean: A man knocks at midnight to borrow bread for a guest; his friend will not get up for friendship’s sake, ‘yet because of the man’s persistence, he will get up and give him as much as he needs.’ ‘Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you.’ No father gives a son a snake for a fish. ‘how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!’
11.big: Pray boldly and persistently; the Father is far more willing than a sleepy neighbour, and his best gift is the Holy Spirit.

11.ctx: ‘The finger of God’ recalls the plagues in Egypt (Exodus 8:19). See the note on Mark 3:20.
11.mean: Some say he drives out demons by Beelzebul. A divided kingdom cannot stand. ‘But if I drive out demons by the finger of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you.’ A stronger one overpowers the armed strong man. ‘He who is not with Me is against Me’.
11.big: Jesus’ victories over demons show God’s kingdom has arrived.

11.mean: An evicted spirit returns to find its old house swept and tidy, and brings seven worse spirits. ‘And the final plight of that man is worse than the first.’
11.big: An empty, reformed life is not enough; it must be filled with God.

11.mean: A woman calls out, ‘Blessed is the womb that bore You, and blessed are the breasts that nursed You!’ ‘Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it.’
11.big: The greatest blessing is open to everyone: hearing God’s word and obeying it.
11.diff: Protestants often cite this against excessive honour to Mary. Yet Calvin said the woman’s blessing was not ‘inappropriate’ and that ‘God conferred the highest honor on Mary’; Jesus’ point is that being renewed by God’s Spirit matters far more. Catholic interpreters point out that Mary is pre-eminently one who heard and kept God’s word (1:38, 45; 2:19, 51), so Jesus’ words describe her too. Both agree Jesus redirects attention to obedience.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 11:27–28 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Catechism of the Catholic Church 966 and 971 (the Assumption; devotion to Mary)

11.mean: ‘This is a wicked generation. It demands a sign, but none will be given it except the sign of Jonah.’ The Queen of the South and the men of Nineveh will condemn it, ‘and now One greater than Solomon is here’, ‘One greater than Jonah is here.’
11.big: Jesus himself, crucified and risen, is God’s sign.

11.mean: A lamp is set on a stand. ‘Your eye is the lamp of your body.’ A good eye fills you with light, a bad one with darkness. ‘Be careful, then, that the light within you is not darkness.’
11.big: Be careful what governs your inner life.

11.h: Woes to Pharisees and Experts in the Law
11.ctx: See the note on Matthew 23:1. Walking over an unmarked grave made a Jew unclean without knowing it.
11.mean: At a Pharisee’s dinner, Jesus does not wash ritually first. ‘Now you Pharisees clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside you are full of greed and wickedness.’ ‘Woe to you Pharisees! For you pay tithes of mint, rue, and every herb, but you disregard justice and the love of God.’ They are ‘like unmarked graves’. The experts in the law load others with burdens, honour the prophets their fathers killed, and ‘have taken away the key to knowledge.’ From then on they oppose him bitterly.
11.big: God looks at the heart; outward religion that ignores justice and love is hollow.

12.ctx: ‘Many thousands’ had gathered; yet Jesus speaks first to his disciples.
12.mean: ‘Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.’ Everything hidden will be revealed; what is whispered will be shouted from the housetops.
12.big: Hypocrisy is pointless, because nothing stays hidden from God.

12.mean: ‘I tell you, My friends, do not be afraid of those who kill the body and after that can do no more.’ Fear the one who ‘has authority to throw you into hell.’ Five sparrows sell for two pennies, ‘Yet not one of them is forgotten by God.’ ‘So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows.’
12.big: Fear of God frees us from fear of people, because he cares for us in every detail.

12.ctx: See the notes on Matthew 10:32 and Mark 3:28.
12.mean: Whoever confesses Jesus before men, ‘the Son of Man will also confess him before the angels of God.’ Speaking against the Son of Man can be forgiven, but not blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. When on trial, ‘the Holy Spirit will teach you what you should say.’
12.big: Stand by Jesus publicly; the Spirit will help you.

12.h: The Parable of the Rich Fool
12.ctx: Rabbis were sometimes asked to settle disputes about inheritance.
12.mean: A man asks Jesus to make his brother share the inheritance. ‘Man, who appointed Me judge or executor between you?’ ‘Watch out! Guard yourselves against every form of greed, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.’ A rich farmer plans bigger barns: ‘Take it easy. Eat, drink, and be merry!’ ‘But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life will be required of you. Then who will own what you have accumulated?’’ ‘This is how it will be for anyone who stores up treasure for himself but is not rich toward God.’
12.big: Life is not measured by possessions; the truly foolish plan for everything except death and God.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 12:13–21 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

12.ctx: See the note on Matthew 6:25. Ravens were unclean birds (Leviticus 11:15), yet God feeds them.
12.mean: ‘Consider the ravens: They do not sow or reap…yet God feeds them. How much more valuable you are than the birds!’ Consider the lilies. ‘your Father knows that you need them. But seek His kingdom, and these things will be added unto you.’
12.big: Trust the Father, and put his kingdom first.

12.ctx: ‘Little flock’ recalls God as Israel’s shepherd.
12.mean: ‘Do not be afraid, little flock, for your Father is pleased to give you the kingdom. Sell your possessions and give to the poor.’ Store up inexhaustible treasure in heaven. ‘For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.’
12.big: Because the Father gives us the kingdom freely, we can give generously.

12.ctx: ‘Dressed for service’ is literally ‘let your loins be girded’: long robes tucked into the belt for action.
12.mean: ‘Be dressed for service and keep your lamps burning.’ Blessed are servants found watching: astonishingly, the master ‘will dress himself to serve and will have them recline at the table, and he himself will come and wait on them.’ ‘You also must be ready, because the Son of Man will come at an hour you do not expect.’ A faithful manager will be rewarded; an abusive one punished. The servant who knew his master’s will and ignored it will be beaten with many blows, the one who did not know, with few. ‘From everyone who has been given much, much will be required’.
12.big: Be ready for Christ’s return by faithful service; greater knowledge brings greater responsibility.
12.diff: Degrees of punishment and reward. Verses 47–48 are a main text for the view, shared across traditions, that judgment will take account of what people knew and were given. Wesley: ‘his having much knowledge will increase, not lessen, his punishment.’

src.l: John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Luke 12

12.ctx: Jesus’ ‘baptism’ here is his death (compare Mark 10:38).
12.mean: ‘I have come to ignite a fire on the earth, and how I wish it were already kindled! But I have a baptism to undergo, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!’ ‘Do you think that I have come to bring peace to the earth? No, I tell you, but division.’ Families will be divided over him.
12.big: Jesus felt the weight of the coming cross; loyalty to him will divide even families.

12.ctx: In Palestine west winds bring rain from the Mediterranean; south winds bring heat from the desert.
12.mean: You can forecast the weather, ‘You hypocrites! You know how to interpret the appearance of the earth and sky. Why don’t you know how to interpret the present time?’
12.big: The signs of God’s kingdom were as obvious as the weather to anyone willing to see.

12.ctx: Debtors could be imprisoned until their debt was paid.
12.mean: ‘Make every effort to reconcile with your adversary while you are on your way to the magistrate.’ Otherwise you will be thrown in prison, ‘you will not get out until you have paid the very last penny.’
12.big: Settle accounts now, with others and with God, before judgment comes.

13.ctx: Neither event is recorded elsewhere. Pilate’s killing of Galilean pilgrims while they offered sacrifices fits what Josephus records of his brutality. The pool of Siloam was at the south end of Jerusalem.
13.mean: People tell Jesus about Galileans ‘whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.’ ‘Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered this way? No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish.’ The same for the eighteen killed when the tower of Siloam fell.
13.big: Disasters are not proof that victims were worse sinners; they are a call to everyone to repent.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 13:1–9 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Josephus, Jewish War 2.169–177 (Whiston): Pilate’s standards and aqueduct

13.h: The Parable of the Barren Fig Tree
13.ctx: Fig trees were often planted in vineyards. The owner has looked for fruit for three years in vain.
13.mean: A fig tree has borne no fruit for three years. ‘Cut it down!’ The keeper pleads: ‘leave it alone again this year, until I dig around it and fertilize it. If it bears fruit next year, fine. But if not, you can cut it down.’
13.big: God is patient, giving time to repent; but his patience is not endless.

13.mean: On the Sabbath Jesus sees a woman bent double for eighteen years: ‘Woman, you are set free from your disability.’ She straightens and praises God. The synagogue leader objects: there are six days for healing. ‘You hypocrites!’ They untie their animals on the Sabbath; ‘Then should not this daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has kept bound for eighteen long years, be released from her bondage on the Sabbath day?’
13.big: The Sabbath is the perfect day for setting people free.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 13:10–17 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

13.h: The Parable of the Mustard Seed
13.mean: ‘It is like a mustard seed that a man tossed into his garden. It grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air nested in its branches.’
13.big: The kingdom grows from tiny beginnings.

13.mean: ‘It is like leaven that a woman took and mixed into three measures of flour, until all of it was leavened.’

13.ctx: A banquet hall door would be shut once the guests had arrived.
13.mean: ‘Lord,’ someone asked Him, ‘will only a few people be saved?’ Jesus turns the question back: ‘Make every effort to enter through the narrow door.’ When the master shuts the door, some will knock: ‘We ate and drank with you, and you taught in our streets.’ ‘I tell you, I do not know where you are from. Depart from me, all you evildoers.’ People will come from east, west, north and south to the kingdom, while some who expected to be there are thrown out. ‘some who are last will be first, and some who are first will be last.’
13.big: Instead of speculating how many will be saved, make sure you enter.

13.ctx: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea, where Jesus was travelling. A fox was a picture of craftiness, and of insignificance.
13.mean: Pharisees warn, ‘Herod wants to kill You.’ ‘Go tell that fox’, Jesus will finish his work on his own timetable: ‘it is not admissible for a prophet to perish outside of Jerusalem.’ ‘O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets…how often I have longed to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!’
13.big: Jesus is not driven by threats; he goes to Jerusalem to die, grieving over the city that rejects him.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 13:31–33 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
‘Herod Antipas’, Lexham Bible Dictionary (citing Hoehner, Herod Antipas)

14.h: Jesus Heals a Man with Dropsy
14.ctx: Dropsy (oedema) is swelling caused by fluid retention, a symptom of serious illness. Found only in Luke.
14.mean: At a leading Pharisee’s Sabbath meal, a man with dropsy is there. ‘Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath or not?’ Silence. Jesus heals him: ‘Which of you whose son or ox falls into a pit on the Sabbath day will not immediately pull him out?’ They cannot answer.

14.ctx: Proverbs 25:6–7 gives similar advice about honour at a king’s table.
14.mean: Seeing guests grab the best seats, Jesus says: take the lowest place, so the host may say, ‘Friend, move up to a better place.’ ‘For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted.’ To the host: do not invite those who can repay you; ‘But when you host a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind, and you will be blessed. Since they cannot repay you, you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.’
14.big: God’s kingdom reverses status; give to those who cannot give back.

14.ctx: See also Matthew 22:1. The guests had already been invited; the servant now tells them the meal is ready. Their excuses are thin.
14.mean: ‘Blessed is everyone who will eat at the feast in the kingdom of God.’ Jesus tells of a great banquet: the invited guests make excuses, a field, oxen, a new wife. The angry master sends his servant to bring in ‘the poor, the crippled, the blind, and the lame.’ There is still room: ‘Go out to the highways and hedges and compel them to come in, so that my house will be full.’
14.big: Those who think they are sure of a place may exclude themselves; God fills his feast with the outcasts.
14.diff: ‘Compel them to come in’ was used by Augustine to justify state pressure against the Donatist schismatics in North Africa (Letter 185), and later to defend religious coercion. Calvin took the words mainly of the Gospel’s earnest pleading, but added that he did ‘not disapprove’ of Augustine’s use of them to justify godly rulers’ edicts. Wesley disagreed: compel ‘With all the violence of love, and the force of God’s word. Such compulsion, and such only, in matters of religion, was used by Christ and his apostles.’ Christians today, Reformed included, almost all reject forcing faith; the compulsion is the urgency of the invitation to people who think they would not be welcome.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 14:15–24 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Augustine, Letter 185 (The Correction of the Donatists) 24, NPNF1 vol. 4, New Advent
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Luke 14

14.ctx: ‘Hate’ in Hebrew idiom often means ‘love less’ (compare Genesis 29:30–31; Matthew 10:37). Wesley: ‘Comparatively to Christ’.
14.mean: ‘If anyone comes to Me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters—yes, even his own life—he cannot be My disciple.’ Count the cost, like a builder planning a tower or a king facing an army. ‘In the same way, any one of you who does not give up everything he has cannot be My disciple.’
14.big: Jesus asks for first place over every other love; count the cost before you follow.

src.l: John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Luke 14

14.mean: Salt that loses its savour is useless, ‘fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile’. ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear.’
14.big: A disciple who loses distinctiveness is useless.

15.h: The Parable of the Lost Sheep
15.ctx: Eating with someone signalled acceptance. The three parables of chapter 15 answer the Pharisees’ complaint.
15.mean: Tax collectors and sinners gather to hear Jesus. The Pharisees grumble: ‘This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.’ Jesus asks: what shepherd would not leave ninety-nine to find one lost sheep, carry it home on his shoulders and call his friends to rejoice? ‘I tell you that in the same way there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous ones who do not need to repent.’
15.big: God seeks the lost and heaven celebrates when one is found.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 15:1–10 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

15.h: The Parable of the Lost Coin
15.ctx: A drachma was about a day’s wage (BSB footnote). Houses were dark with few windows.
15.mean: A woman loses one of ten silver coins, lights a lamp, sweeps and searches until she finds it, and calls her friends to rejoice. ‘In the same way, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of God’s angels over one sinner who repents.’
15.big: God searches carefully for what is lost and rejoices when it is found.

15.h: The Parable of the Prodigal Son
15.ctx: Asking for his share while his father was still alive was shocking. Pigs were unclean animals (Leviticus 11:7); feeding them was about as low as a Jew could sink.
15.mean: A younger son takes his share, squanders it ‘in wild living’, and ends up feeding pigs, starving. ‘Finally he came to his senses’ and goes home to say, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ ‘But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with compassion. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.’ The father calls for the best robe, a ring, sandals and the fattened calf: ‘For this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was lost and is found!’ The older son, who has ‘never disobeyed’, is angry and will not go in. The father pleads with him too: ‘Son, you are always with me,’ ‘and all that is mine is yours. But it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’
15.big: God the Father runs to welcome repentant sinners with lavish grace; the story ends asking whether the ‘older brothers’, the religious, will join the celebration.
15.diff: Some have argued that because the father forgives without any sacrifice, the parable shows no need for the cross. Most interpreters reply that a parable makes one point, here the Father’s welcome of sinners, and that Jesus is telling it on his way to Jerusalem to die; the cost of the welcome is shown elsewhere (for example 22:20; 24:46–47). Calvin saw in the father ‘the boundless goodness and inestimable forbearance of God, that no crimes, however aggravated, may deter us from the hope of obtaining pardon’.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 15:11–32 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

16.h: The Parable of the Shrewd Manager
16.ctx: A manager (steward) ran an estate for a wealthy owner and could act in his name. The amounts are huge: a hundred measures of olive oil was about 3,300 litres (BSB footnote).
16.mean: A manager about to be sacked for waste calls in his master’s debtors and quietly cuts their bills, so they will welcome him later. ‘The master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly.’ ‘For the sons of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own kind than are the sons of light.’ ‘I tell you, use worldly wealth to make friends for yourselves so that when it is gone, they will welcome you into eternal dwellings.’ Faithfulness in small things shows faithfulness in great. ‘You cannot serve both God and money.’
16.big: Jesus does not praise the cheating but the foresight: use money now, generously, with eternity in view.
16.diff: This is one of the hardest parables. Calvin warned that ‘to inquire with great exactness into every minute part of a parable is an absurd mode of philosophizing’; its point is that we should ‘deal kindly and generously with our neighbors’. He added that Christ is not advising us to buy forgiveness with gifts. Wesley read ‘make friends’ as doing good, especially to God’s children, who will welcome us in heaven.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 16:1–15 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Luke 16

16.ctx: ‘Everyone is forcing his way into it’ may also be translated ‘everyone is urged to enter into it’ (BSB footnote). See the note on Mark 10:1 on divorce.
16.mean: The Pharisees, ‘who were lovers of money’, scoff. ‘You are the ones who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts. For what is prized among men is detestable before God.’ ‘The Law and the Prophets were proclaimed until John. Since that time, the gospel of the kingdom of God is being preached’. Yet the Law has not been cancelled: ‘it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for a single stroke of a pen to drop out of the Law.’ Divorcing a wife to marry another is adultery.
16.big: God sees the heart behind outward respectability. John marks the turning point: the kingdom has come; but God’s law, including his design for marriage, still stands.

src.l: John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Luke 16

16.ctx: Purple dye was extremely expensive; it marked royalty and great wealth. ‘Abraham’s side’ is literally ‘Abraham’s bosom’ (BSB footnote), a picture of honoured fellowship at a feast. Hades is the realm of the dead. This Lazarus is the only person named in any of Jesus’ parables; he is not Lazarus of Bethany (John 11).
16.mean: A rich man feasts every day; the beggar Lazarus lies at his gate, covered with sores, licked by dogs. Both die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham’s side; the rich man is in torment in Hades. He begs for Lazarus to cool his tongue. ‘Child, remember that during your lifetime you received your good things, while Lazarus received bad things.’ ‘a great chasm has been fixed between us and you’. He begs that Lazarus warn his five brothers. ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let your brothers listen to them.’ ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.’
16.big: Death fixes our destiny; how we treat the poor shows whether we have listened to God’s word; and miracles will not convince those who refuse Scripture.
16.diff: Parable or real event? Calvin: ‘Some look upon it as a simple parable; but, as the name Lazarus occurs in it, I rather consider it to be the narrative of an actual fact. But that is of little consequence’. Most readers today treat it as a parable, and so are cautious about drawing a detailed map of the afterlife from it. What it shows about life after death. Reformed, Catholic, Orthodox and Wesleyan teaching all cite it for conscious existence immediately after death (see the glossary entry intermediate state); Catholics also see in it the particular judgment at death (Catechism 1021). Seventh-day Adventists, who hold that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection, read it as a parable using familiar images, not as teaching. Praying to the departed? Wesley noted that the rich man’s request to Abraham is ‘one precedent in Scripture of praying to departed saints: but who is it that prays, and with what success?’

17.ctx: See the note on Matthew 18:6. A millstone was a heavy stone for grinding grain.
17.mean: Stumbling blocks will come, ‘but woe to the one through whom they come!’ ‘Watch yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him.’ Even seven times in a day.
17.big: Take sin seriously, your own and others’; and keep forgiving.

17.ctx: A slave who had worked in the field all day was still expected to serve his master’s meal.
17.mean: ‘Increase our faith!’ Faith as small as a mustard seed could uproot a mulberry tree. A servant does not expect thanks for doing his duty: ‘So you also, when you have done everything commanded of you, should say, ‘We are unworthy servants; we have only done our duty.’’
17.big: It is not the size of faith that matters but the God it trusts; and obedience earns us no claim on God.
17.diff: Can we earn anything from God? Calvin: our zeal ‘does not lay him under obligation to us by any sort of merit’. Wesley agreed ‘a man cannot profit God’, yet added that God ‘is pleased to give by his grace a value to our good works, which in consequence of his promise entitles us to an eternal reward.’ Catholic teaching says ‘there is no strict right to any merit on the part of man’, yet God freely makes it possible: ‘the merit of good works is to be attributed in the first place to the grace of God, then to the faithful’ (Catechism 2007–2008). All agree that any reward is God’s gift, not something he owes us; they differ over whether to call it ‘merit’.

17.ctx: Lepers had to live apart and keep their distance (Leviticus 13:45–46). A healed leper had to be inspected by a priest (Leviticus 14). Jews and Samaritans normally kept apart, but shared misery had brought these men together.
17.mean: Ten lepers call from a distance, ‘Jesus, Master, have mercy on us!’ ‘Go, show yourselves to the priests.’ On the way they are cleansed. One comes back praising God and falls at Jesus’ feet—‘and he was a Samaritan.’ ‘Were not all ten cleansed?’ ‘Where then are the other nine?’ ‘Rise and go; your faith has made you well!’
17.big: Ten received healing; only one, an outsider, returned to give thanks, and heard the deeper word that his faith had saved him (BSB footnote: ‘has saved you’).

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 17:11–21 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

17.ctx: ‘In your midst’ may also be translated ‘within you’ or ‘within your grasp’ (BSB footnote). Jesus is speaking to Pharisees. See the note on Matthew 24:36 for ‘one will be taken’.
17.mean: ‘The kingdom of God will not come with observable signs.’ ‘For you see, the kingdom of God is in your midst.’ To the disciples: do not chase rumours of the Son of Man; his day will be as plain as lightning. ‘But first He must suffer many things and be rejected by this generation.’ People will be going about ordinary life, as in the days of Noah and Lot. ‘Remember Lot’s wife!’ ‘one will be taken and the other left.’
17.big: The kingdom is already present in Jesus; its full coming will be sudden and unmistakable, so be ready and do not look back.
17.diff: ‘Within you’ or ‘among you’? Calvin took it inwardly: the kingdom is ‘nothing else than the inward and spiritual renewal’ of the soul. Wesley allowed both: ‘within or among you…it is now in the midst of you’. Many modern versions prefer ‘among you’, since Jesus is speaking to Pharisees who opposed him, and the king himself was standing in front of them.

18.h: The Parable of the Persistent Widow
18.ctx: Widows were among the most vulnerable people, often without a man to defend them in court (Exodus 22:22; Isaiah 1:17).
18.mean: Jesus told them a parable ‘about their need to pray at all times and not lose heart’. An unjust judge finally gives a widow justice just to stop her pestering. ‘Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night?’ ‘Nevertheless, when the Son of Man comes, will He find faith on earth?’
18.big: If even a bad judge yields to persistence, how much more will our just and loving Father answer his children; so keep praying.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 18:1–8 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

18.h: The Pharisee and the Tax Collector
18.ctx: Pharisees were respected for their devotion; the law required only one annual fast (the Day of Atonement), but some Pharisees fasted twice a week. Tax collectors were seen as traitors and cheats.
18.mean: Jesus speaks ‘To some who trusted in their own righteousness and viewed others with contempt’. The Pharisee prays, ‘God, I thank You that I am not like other men’. ‘But the tax collector stood at a distance, unwilling even to lift up his eyes to heaven. Instead, he beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner!’’ ‘I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified.’
18.big: God accepts not the one who trusts in his own goodness but the one who throws himself on God’s mercy.
18.diff: Justification. Everyone agrees the tax collector went home right with God by mercy, not merit. Traditions differ on what ‘justified’ involves. Reformed and Lutheran: God declares sinners righteous ‘not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous’ for Christ’s sake, received by faith (Westminster Confession 11.1). Calvin warned that anyone who ‘imagines the righteousness of those works to be the cause of his salvation, or rests upon it, he is condemned for wicked arrogance’. Wesleyan: Wesley noted ‘justified rather than the other’ means ‘and not the other’. Catholic: ‘Justification is not only the remission of sins, but also the sanctification and renewal of the interior man’; it is ‘merited for us by the Passion of Christ’ and makes us ‘inwardly just’ (Catechism 1989, 1992).

18.ctx: See the note on Mark 10:13. Luke says these were ‘babies’.
18.mean: Parents bring babies for Jesus to touch; the disciples rebuke them. ‘Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them! For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.’ ‘anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.’
18.big: The kingdom is received as a gift, by the helpless, not earned by the accomplished.

18.ctx: See the note on Mark 10:17 (including the ‘eye of a needle’).
18.mean: ‘Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?’ ‘No one is good except God alone.’ He claims he has kept the commandments. ‘You still lack one thing: Sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.’ He goes away very sad. ‘How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!’ ‘Who then can be saved?’ ‘What is impossible with man is possible with God.’
18.big: Salvation is impossible for us and possible only by God; wealth can keep us from following Jesus.

18.h: The Third Prediction of the Passion
18.mean: ‘everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled.’ He will be handed to the Gentiles, mocked, flogged and killed, ‘and on the third day He will rise again.’ ‘The meaning was hidden from them’.
18.big: Jesus’ death fulfils Scripture; understanding it is God’s gift (24:45).

18.ctx: See the note on Mark 10:46. Luke places the healing as Jesus approaches Jericho; Mark as he leaves it.
18.mean: A blind man shouts, ‘Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!’ Rebuked, he cries ‘all the louder’. ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’ ‘Lord,’ he said, ‘let me see again.’ ‘Receive your sight!’ Jesus replied. ‘Your faith has healed you.’ He follows Jesus, glorifying God.
18.big: The blind beggar sees who Jesus is (Son of David) when many sighted people do not.

19.ctx: Zacchaeus was a ‘chief tax collector’, in charge of others, who could collect more than Rome required and keep the extra. The Law required fourfold repayment for a stolen sheep (Exodus 22:1).
19.mean: Zacchaeus, small and rich, climbs a sycamore to see Jesus. ‘Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today.’ He welcomes Jesus joyfully; the crowd grumbles, ‘He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!’ ‘Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.’ ‘Today salvation has come to this house, because this man too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.’
19.big: Jesus seeks the lost before they deserve it; real conversion shows itself in changed handling of money and in putting wrongs right.
19.diff: Calvin: Zacchaeus’ generosity ‘proceeded from that living root’ of inward repentance: ‘We ought therefore to begin with the heart, but our repentance ought also to be evinced by works.’ All traditions see Zacchaeus as a model of repentance and restitution.

b: New Testament Jericho was not on the ancient mound of Joshua’s day (Tell es-Sultan) but nearby, beside the Wadi Qelt (Tulul Abu el-‘Alayiq). There the Hasmonean kings, and then Herod the Great, built winter palaces with pools and gardens. Excavations have uncovered Herod’s palace complexes, which spread across both sides of the wadi. It was a wealthy town on the road from Galilee and Perea to Jerusalem, and a natural place for a chief tax collector to live.

19.h: The Parable of the Ten Minas
19.ctx: A mina was about a hundred days’ wages (BSB footnote). Compare the talents in Matthew 25:14; here each servant receives the same.
19.mean: People thought ‘the kingdom of God would appear imminently.’ A nobleman goes away to receive a kingdom, giving ten servants a mina each: ‘Conduct business with this until I return’. His subjects reject him. On his return one servant has made ten minas: ‘Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful in a very small matter, you shall have authority over ten cities.’ Another, afraid, hid his mina in a cloth; it is taken from him. The rebels are judged.
19.big: Between Jesus’ going and his return, his servants must work faithfully with what he has entrusted to them; and those who reject his rule will face him as king.

hist.t: A king who went to a far country
b: When Herod the Great died in 4 BC, his will left Judea and Samaria to his son Archelaus, who went to Rome to have the emperor Augustus confirm it. Josephus records that fifty Jewish envoys, backed by thousands of Jews living in Rome, went before Augustus to accuse him. Augustus ratified the will, but Archelaus ruled from 4 BC to AD 6 without the title of king, and his harsh rule ended when he was deposed and banished.

This history is well established. Whether Jesus meant his hearers to think of it is a matter of interpretation, but the likeness is striking: a nobleman goes ‘to a distant country to lay claim to his kingship’, and his subjects send a delegation saying, ‘We do not want this man to rule over us.’

19.ctx: See the note on Mark 11:1. Luke omits ‘Hosanna’ and the palm branches; he alone records the Pharisees’ protest.
19.mean: Jesus rides a colt down the Mount of Olives. The disciples praise God: ‘Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord!’ ‘Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!’ ‘Teacher, rebuke Your disciples!’ ‘I tell you,’ He answered, ‘if they remain silent, the very stones will cry out.’
19.big: Jesus openly accepts praise as the promised King.

19.ctx: Found only in Luke. Fulfilled when the Romans besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70 (see the note on 21:20).
19.mean: Seeing the city, Jesus weeps: ‘If only you had known on this day what would bring you peace! But now it is hidden from your eyes.’ Enemies will surround it and ‘will not leave one stone on another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.’
19.big: Jesus grieves over those who reject him, even while announcing their judgment.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 19:41–44 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

19.mean: He drives out the sellers: ‘It is written: ‘My house will be a house of prayer.’ But you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’’ He teaches daily in the temple; the leaders want to kill him, but ‘all the people hung on His words.’
19.big: Jesus claims authority over God’s house.

20.mean: ‘Tell us,’ they said, ‘by what authority are You doing these things, and who gave You this authority?’ Jesus asks about John’s baptism; they will not answer. ‘Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.’
20.big: Those who refuse the evidence they have will not be given more.

20.h: The Parable of the Wicked Tenants
20.mean: Tenants beat the owner’s servants. ‘I will send my beloved son. Perhaps they will respect him.’ They kill him. The owner ‘will come and kill those tenants and give the vineyard to others.’ ‘The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone’.
20.big: Jesus is the Father’s beloved Son, rejected but vindicated.

20.mean: Spies try to trap him. ‘Is it lawful for us to pay taxes to Caesar or not?’ ‘Show Me a denarius. Whose image and inscription are on it?’ ‘Give to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.’
20.big: Give the state its due, and give God everything, since we bear his image.

20.mean: Sadducees, ‘who say there is no resurrection’, pose a puzzle about a widow of seven brothers. Those raised ‘will neither marry nor be given in marriage. In fact, they can no longer die, because they are like the angels.’ God is ‘the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.’ ‘He is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for to Him all are alive.’
20.big: The resurrection life is real and transformed; those who belong to God are alive to him.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 20:27–40 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

20.mean: ‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet.”’ ‘Thus David calls Him ‘Lord.’ So how can He be David’s son?’
20.big: The Messiah is David’s son and David’s Lord.

20.mean: ‘Beware of the scribes.’ They love long robes, greetings and the best seats. ‘They defraud widows of their houses, and for a show make lengthy prayers. These men will receive greater condemnation.’
20.big: Religious show combined with exploiting the weak brings greater judgment.

21.ctx: See the note on Mark 12:41. Two lepta were the smallest coins in use (BSB footnote).
21.mean: Jesus watches the rich giving and a poor widow put in two tiny coins. ‘Truly I tell you,’ He said, ‘this poor widow has put in more than all the others. For they all contributed out of their surplus, but she out of her poverty has put in all she had to live on.’
21.big: God measures a gift by what it costs the giver and the trust behind it.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 21:1–4 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

21.ctx: See the note and history drop-down on Mark 13:1.
21.mean: Some admire the temple’s beautiful stones. ‘the time will come when not one stone will be left on another’. When? ‘See to it that you are not deceived.’ Many will come claiming, ‘I am He,’ and, ‘The time is near.’ ‘Do not follow them.’ Wars must come, ‘but the end is not imminent.’
21.big: Do not be deceived by false messiahs or date-setters.

21.ctx: Acts records many of these trials: before synagogues, prisons, kings and governors (Acts 4–5; 12; 24–26).
21.mean: Wars, earthquakes, famines and signs will come. ‘But before all this, they will seize you and persecute you.’ ‘This will be your opportunity to serve as witnesses.’ ‘For I will give you speech and wisdom that none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict.’ Some will be betrayed and killed, ‘Yet not even a hair of your head will perish. By your patient endurance you will gain your souls.’
21.big: Persecution is an opportunity to witness; Christ gives words, and keeps his people eternally safe.

21.ctx: Luke speaks plainly of armies surrounding Jerusalem, where Mark has ‘the abomination of desolation’ (Mark 13:14). The Romans besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70: see the history drop-down at Mark 13:1, which also records the flight of the Jerusalem church to Pella.
21.mean: ‘But when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, you will know that her desolation is near.’ Flee to the mountains. ‘For these are the days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written.’ ‘And Jerusalem will be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled.’
21.big: Jesus foretold Jerusalem’s fall and told his followers how to escape it; God’s word comes true.
21.diff: Scholars who date Luke after AD 70 often point to this verse, arguing that it reflects the siege; others reply that siege was simply how cities were taken, and that the description stays general. See the drop-down ‘When was it written?’ in the introduction. ‘The times of the Gentiles’. Some see this as the whole church age; many also see in ‘until’ a hint of future hope for Israel (compare Romans 11:25–26).

21.h: The Return of the Son of Man
21.ctx: See the note on Mark 13:24. Daniel 7:13–14 lies behind ‘coming in a cloud’.
21.mean: Signs in the sun, moon and stars; nations in anguish. ‘At that time they will see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and great glory. When these things begin to happen, stand up and lift up your heads, because your redemption is drawing near.’
21.big: What terrifies the world is, for believers, a sign that rescue is near.

21.h: The Lesson of the Fig Tree
21.ctx: See the note on Mark 13:28 on ‘this generation’.
21.mean: When trees sprout leaves, summer is near; ‘when you see these things happening, know that the kingdom of God is near.’ ‘Truly I tell you, this generation will not pass away until all these things have happened. Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away.’
21.big: Jesus’ words are more permanent than the universe.
21.diff: Wesley took ‘all these things’ to mean ‘All that has been spoken of the destruction of Jerusalem’.

src.l: John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Luke 21

21.ctx: The Mount of Olives faces the temple across the Kidron valley.
21.mean: ‘But watch yourselves, or your hearts will be weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the worries of life—and that day will spring upon you suddenly like a snare.’ ‘So keep watch at all times, and pray’. Each day Jesus taught in the temple and spent nights on the Mount of Olives.
21.big: Not only wild living but ordinary anxieties can dull us; watch and pray.

22.mean: Passover approaches; the chief priests and scribes look for a way to kill Jesus, ‘for they feared the people.’
22.big: Jesus’ enemies plan in secret, but God is working to his own timetable.

22.mean: ‘Then Satan entered Judas Iscariot, who was one of the Twelve.’ He agrees with the chief priests to betray Jesus for money ‘in the absence of a crowd.’
22.big: Satan is at work, and Judas is responsible; neither defeats God’s purpose (22:22).

22.mean: Jesus sends Peter and John: a man carrying a jug of water will lead them to a house with ‘a large upper room, already furnished.’ ‘So they went and found it just as Jesus had told them.’
22.big: Jesus is in control of every detail of his final days.

22.ctx: Luke mentions two cups; the Passover meal used several. ‘Some manuscripts end verse 19 after This is My body and do not include verse 20’ (BSB footnote); most modern translations include the full text, which closely matches Paul in 1 Corinthians 11:23–25.
22.mean: ‘I have eagerly desired to eat this Passover with you before My suffering.’ He shares a cup. ‘And He took the bread, gave thanks and broke it, and gave it to them, saying, “This is My body, given for you; do this in remembrance of Me.”’ ‘This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you.’ The betrayer is at the table. ‘Indeed, the Son of Man will go as it has been determined, but woe to that man who betrays Him.’
22.big: Jesus gives his church a meal to remember his body given and blood poured out for us, sealing the new covenant.
22.diff: For the main Christian views of Christ’s presence in the Supper, see the note on Mark 14:17 and the glossary. Wesley read ‘This is my body’ as ‘figurative language’, like calling the lamb ‘the passover’. Only Luke and Paul record ‘do this in remembrance of Me’; all traditions keep the command, while differing on what ‘remembrance’ involves.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Luke 22:17–20 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

22.ctx: Rulers liked the title ‘Benefactor’ (Greek euergetes), advertising their generosity. Compare Mark 10:42.
22.mean: Even at the Supper the disciples argue about who is greatest. ‘The kings of the Gentiles lord it over them’. ‘But you shall not be like them.’ ‘But I am among you as one who serves.’ Yet he gives them a kingdom: they will eat at his table and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.
22.big: In Christ’s kingdom, leaders serve, as he did.

22.ctx: ‘You’ in verse 31 is plural (‘all of you’); ‘you’ in verse 32 is singular, Peter. Wheat was sifted by shaking it to separate grain from chaff.
22.mean: ‘Simon, Simon, Satan has asked to sift all of you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.’ Peter protests he is ready for prison and death. ‘I tell you, Peter, the rooster will not crow today until you have denied three times that you know Me.’
22.big: Satan sifts, but Jesus prays; a failing disciple can be restored and used to strengthen others.
22.diff: Catholic teaching links this verse with Matthew 16:18–19: Peter’s ‘mission will be to keep this faith from every lapse and to strengthen his brothers in it’ (Catechism 552), a role it sees continued in the bishop of Rome. Protestant readers see Jesus’ personal care for Peter, who would fall and be restored (John 21:15–19). Wesley: ‘that thy faith fail not’ means ‘Altogether’, and the ‘brethren’ are ‘all that are weak in faith’. See the note on Matthew 16:13.

22.ctx: ‘And He was numbered with the transgressors’ quotes Isaiah 53:12. Many travellers carried a short sword against robbers.
22.mean: Before, they lacked nothing. ‘Now, however,’ He told them, ‘the one with a purse should take it, and likewise a bag; and the one without a sword should sell his cloak and buy one.’ Scripture must be fulfilled: he will be counted among criminals. ‘Look, Lord, here are two swords.’ ‘That is enough,’ He answered.
22.big: Jesus warns that hostile days are coming as he goes to die among the lawless; the disciples misunderstand him.
22.diff: A verse once used for church power. Pope Boniface VIII, in Unam Sanctam (1302), read the two swords as ‘the spiritual and the temporal’, both ‘in the power of the Church’. Calvin called the disciples’ reply ‘shameful and stupid ignorance’ of the cross and rejected that reading. Wesley: ‘It is plain, this is not to be taken literally’; ‘It is enough’ means ‘I did not mean literally, that every one of you must have a sword’. The Catholic Church today teaches that it ‘is not to be confused in any way with the political community’ (Catechism 2245). Most interpreters read ‘That is enough’ as Jesus ending a conversation they had misunderstood; a few minutes later he stops the use of a sword (22:51).

22.h: Jesus Prays on the Mount of Olives
22.ctx: See the note and history drop-down on Mark 14:32 (Gethsemane). ‘Some manuscripts do not include verses 43 and 44’ (BSB footnote); but Justin Martyr (about AD 155) knew the bloody sweat from the apostles’ ‘memoirs’, and Irenaeus (about AD 180) cited it as proof that Jesus had a real human body.
22.mean: ‘Pray that you will not enter into temptation.’ Kneeling, Jesus prays, ‘Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done.’ ‘Then an angel from heaven appeared to Him and strengthened Him. And in His anguish, He prayed more earnestly, and His sweat became like drops of blood falling to the ground.’ He finds the disciples ‘asleep, exhausted from sorrow.’
22.big: Jesus truly dreaded the cup of God’s judgment, and still chose the Father’s will, for us.
22.diff: See the note on Mark 14:32 on Christ’s two wills. Wesley saw Jesus ‘grappling with the powers of darkness: feeling the weight of the wrath of God’.

22.ctx: See the notes on Mark 14:43 and Matthew 26:47. Only Luke records the healing of the ear.
22.mean: Judas comes to kiss Jesus: ‘Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?’ A disciple cuts off the high priest’s servant’s right ear. ‘No more of this!’ And He touched the man’s ear and healed him. ‘But this hour belongs to you and to the power of darkness.’
22.big: Even while being arrested, Jesus heals an enemy and refuses violence.

22.mean: Three times Peter denies knowing Jesus. While he is still speaking the rooster crows. ‘And the Lord turned and looked at Peter.’ Peter remembers, ‘And he went outside and wept bitterly.’
22.big: Jesus’ look was not the end for Peter but the start of repentance.

22.ctx: Blindfolding and striking was a cruel game mocking his claim to be a prophet.
22.mean: The guards blindfold and beat him: ‘Prophesy! Who hit You?’
22.big: The true Prophet is mocked by those who cannot see.

22.ctx: See the note and history drop-downs on Mark 14:53. Luke describes a formal morning session.
22.mean: ‘If You are the Christ, tell us.’ ‘But from now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.’ ‘Are You then the Son of God?’ He replied, ‘You say that I am.’ ‘We have heard it for ourselves from His own lips.’
22.big: Jesus is condemned for telling the truth about himself: Messiah, Son of Man, Son of God.

23.ctx: See the note and history drop-down on Mark 15:1.
23.mean: They accuse him of ‘subverting our nation, forbidding payment of taxes to Caesar’ (compare 20:25) and claiming to be a king. ‘Are You the King of the Jews?’ ‘You have said so,’ ‘I find no basis for a charge against this man.’
23.big: Political charges are invented; Pilate himself finds Jesus innocent.

b: Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36/37 and is one of the best-attested figures of the period. Josephus describes him bringing Roman standards bearing the emperor’s image into Jerusalem by night, backing down when crowds offered to die rather than see their law broken, and later using temple funds for an aqueduct and having protesters clubbed. The Roman historian Tacitus writes that ‘Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of the procurator Pontius Pilatus’.

The Pilate Stone. In 1961 Italian archaeologists excavating the theatre at Caesarea Maritima found a reused limestone block with a Latin inscription recording that Pilate dedicated a building in honour of the emperor Tiberius. It gives his title as ‘prefect of Judea’ and is now in the Israel Museum, Jerusalem.

23.ctx: Found only in Luke. Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and happened to be in Jerusalem. See also 9:9 and 13:31.
23.mean: Herod is pleased, hoping to see a miracle. He questions Jesus at length, ‘but He gave no answer.’ Herod and his soldiers mock him, dress him in a fine robe and send him back. ‘That day Herod and Pilate became friends; before this time they had been enemies.’
23.big: Jesus has nothing to say to curiosity without repentance; and opposition to him unites old enemies.

hist.t: Herod Antipas, Herodias and John’s death
b: The ‘King Herod’ of Mark 6 is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. After his father died in 4 BC, Augustus made him tetrarch (ruler of a quarter) of Galilee and Perea, which he governed for 43 years. Matthew and Luke give his exact title, ‘tetrarch’; Mark uses the popular ‘king’. He rebuilt Sepphoris and founded Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee.

Josephus confirms the outline of Mark’s account. Antipas divorced his first wife, daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, to marry Herodias, who had been married to his half-brother. Josephus calls that first husband Herod; Mark calls him Philip. Since several of Herod the Great’s sons were called Herod, some suggest he bore both names. Aretas later defeated Antipas in battle, and Josephus says many Jews saw the defeat as God’s punishment for his killing of ‘John, that was called the Baptist’, ‘a good man’ who called the Jews to righteousness and baptism.

Josephus gives a political reason for the execution: Antipas feared John’s influence over the crowds might lead to a revolt. Mark gives the personal story. The two fit together easily. Josephus says John was held and killed at Machaerus, Antipas’s fortress east of the Dead Sea.

23.ctx: See the note and history drop-down on Mark 15:6. Luke stresses that Pilate declared Jesus innocent three times (23:4, 14, 22).
23.mean: ‘He has done nothing deserving of death.’ The crowd shouts, ‘Away with this man! Release Barabbas to us!’, a rebel and murderer. ‘Crucify Him! Crucify Him!’ ‘And their clamor prevailed.’ Pilate releases Barabbas ‘and he handed Jesus over to their will.’
23.big: The innocent one is condemned and the guilty one goes free: a picture of what Jesus does for us.

23.ctx: See the notes and history drop-downs on Mark 15:21 and 15:42. ‘The Skull’ is Greek Kranion, Latin Calvaria, hence ‘Calvary’ (BSB footnote). ‘Some manuscripts do not include’ Jesus’ prayer ‘Father, forgive them’ (BSB footnote); most modern translations keep it in the text.
23.mean: Simon of Cyrene carries the cross. Jesus tells mourning women, ‘Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for Me, but weep for yourselves and for your children.’ He is crucified between two criminals. ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.’ Rulers and soldiers mock: ‘save Yourself!’ One criminal joins in; the other rebukes him: ‘We are punished justly…But this man has done nothing wrong.’ ‘Jesus, remember me when You come into Your kingdom!’ ‘Truly I tell you, today you will be with Me in Paradise.’
23.big: Jesus prays for his killers and promises paradise to a dying criminal who simply trusts him: salvation by grace alone.
23.diff: ‘Today…in Paradise’. Calvin: ‘souls, when they have departed from their bodies, continue to live; otherwise the promise of Christ…would be a mockery.’ Wesley: Paradise is ‘The place where the souls of the righteous remain from death till the resurrection…this very day.’ The Catechism cites it for each person’s destiny being settled at death (1021), and the Westminster Confession teaches the same. Jehovah’s Witnesses, who hold that the dead are unconscious, translate ‘Truly I tell you today, you will be with me in Paradise’, placing the comma after ‘today’. Greek manuscripts had little punctuation, so the grammar allows either; but Jesus regularly says ‘Truly I tell you’ without adding ‘today’, which is why almost all translations put the comma before it. The thief and the sacraments. He was saved without baptism or good works. Traditions that hold baptism to be necessary agree that God can save in such cases: ‘God has bound salvation to the sacrament of Baptism, but he himself is not bound by his sacraments’ (Catechism 1257).

b: Crucifixion was the Romans’ most shameful punishment, used for slaves and rebels. Ancient writers describe it often, but physical remains are rare, because bodies were usually left to decay or thrown away. In 1968, in a tomb at Giv’at ha-Mivtar in northern Jerusalem, archaeologists found an ossuary containing the bones of a crucified man from the 1st century AD, with an iron nail about 11.5 cm long still driven through his heel bone. It confirms that victims were nailed, and that a crucified Jew could be given a proper family burial, as Jesus was.

23.ctx: The sixth to the ninth hour was noon to 3 p.m. (BSB footnote). See the note and history drop-down on Mark 15:33. ‘Into Your hands I commit My Spirit’ quotes Psalm 31:5, a Jewish evening prayer.
23.mean: Darkness covers the land; the temple veil is torn. ‘Father, into Your hands I commit My Spirit.’ He breathes his last. The centurion glorifies God: ‘Surely this was a righteous man.’ The crowds go home beating their breasts; the women from Galilee watch from a distance.
23.big: Jesus dies trusting his Father; even a Roman soldier sees his innocence.

23.ctx: See the note and history drop-down on Mark 15:42. Luke notes that Joseph had not agreed with the Council’s decision.
23.mean: Joseph of Arimathea, ‘a good and righteous man’, asks Pilate for the body and lays it ‘in a tomb cut into the rock, where no one had yet been laid.’ The women from Galilee see the tomb and how the body was placed, and prepare spices. ‘And they rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment.’
23.big: Jesus truly died and was buried, and the women knew exactly where.

hist.t: Where are Golgotha and the tomb?
b: Two sites are shown today.

The Church of the Holy Sepulchre. In the 4th century the emperor Constantine built a church over a site local Christians identified, under a temple Hadrian had built about AD 135. It is now inside the Old City walls, but excavations, including Kathleen Kenyon’s in the 1960s, showed that in Jesus’ time the area was an old quarry outside the walls, with rock-cut tombs of the 1st century. Most archaeologists regard it as the most likely location.

The Garden Tomb. North of the Damascus Gate, identified by General Charles Gordon in 1883, it is a peaceful place to visit. But excavations by Gabriel Barkay and Amos Kloner indicate that the tomb was first cut in the Iron Age (8th–7th centuries BC), so it would not have been a new tomb in Jesus’ day. Few archaeologists now think it was Jesus’ tomb.

24.ctx: See the notes on Mark 16:1 and Matthew 28:1. Joanna was the wife of Herod’s household manager (8:3).
24.mean: The women find the stone rolled away and no body. Two men in dazzling clothes: ‘Why do you look for the living among the dead? He is not here; He has risen!’ They remind them of Jesus’ words. The women tell the apostles, ‘But their words seemed like nonsense to them’. Peter runs to the tomb and sees only the linen cloths.
24.big: The tomb is empty because Jesus is alive, exactly as he said; the disciples were not expecting it.

24.ctx: Cleopas may be the Clopas of John 19:25. The other disciple is unnamed.
24.mean: Two disciples walk home, sad and confused. Jesus joins them, ‘But their eyes were kept from recognizing Him.’ ‘we were hoping He was the One who would redeem Israel.’ ‘O foolish ones, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?’ ‘And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, He explained to them what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself.’ At supper he breaks bread; ‘Then their eyes were opened and they recognized Jesus’, and he vanishes. ‘Were not our hearts burning within us’? They hurry back to Jerusalem: ‘The Lord has indeed risen and has appeared to Simon!’
24.big: The whole Old Testament points to a suffering and glorified Messiah; the risen Jesus is known through the Scriptures and in the breaking of bread.
24.diff: Many readers, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, hear an echo of the Lord’s Supper in ‘the breaking of the bread’ (verse 35; compare Acts 2:42). Others note that the actions are those of any Jewish host at a meal. Calvin stressed that their eyes had been ‘covered’: Jesus did not change his form; God ‘blunted their acuteness’ until the right moment.

b: No site has been identified for certain. Luke puts Emmaus sixty stadia from Jerusalem, about 7 miles (11 km) (BSB footnote).

Nicopolis (‘Amwas’), in the lowlands, is the traditional identification, going back to Eusebius in the 4th century. But it is about 19 miles (160 stadia) from Jerusalem, a distance found only in less reliable manuscripts, and the two disciples would then have walked 19 miles back uphill in the dark and still found the apostles gathered after their meal.

Mozah, a 1st-century village in the hill country near Jerusalem, is about 30 stadia away, the distance Josephus gives for an Emmaus in the hill country. If Luke’s sixty stadia is the round trip, it fits well. The Lexham Bible Dictionary judges it the most likely site.

24.ctx: The disciples were frightened, ‘thinking they had seen a spirit’, a ghost.
24.mean: ‘Peace be with you.’ ‘Look at My hands and My feet. It is I Myself. Touch Me and see—for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have.’ He eats broiled fish in front of them. ‘Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms.’ ‘Then He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures.’ Repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed in his name to all nations. ‘You are witnesses of these things.’ They are to wait for ‘the promise of My Father’, power from on high.
24.big: Jesus rose bodily, not as a ghost; the same Jesus, with a real and glorified body, sends his witnesses to all nations in the Spirit’s power.
24.diff: All the historic creeds confess the bodily resurrection. Calvin: ‘I am clothed with that flesh which was crucified, and which still bears the marks of it.’ Luke stresses physical proofs, touching and eating, which rule out the idea that the disciples saw only a ghost or a vision.

24.ctx: Acts 1:3–11 tells the ascension more fully, forty days after the resurrection; here Luke compresses the time. The words ‘and was carried up into heaven’ are missing from some manuscripts.
24.mean: At Bethany Jesus lifts up his hands and blesses them. ‘While He was blessing them, He left them and was carried up into heaven. And they worshiped Him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, praising God continually in the temple.’
24.big: Luke’s Gospel ends as it began, in the temple, with joy and praise; the ascended Jesus reigns and blesses his people.
24.diff: Wesley: it was fitting that the apostles should see the ascension, since ‘they could not see him in heaven while they continued on earth.’ The New Bible Dictionary notes that the ascension marks the end of the resurrection appearances, and that Christ is now ‘seated, a sign that his atoning work is complete’, and intercedes for his people. See also the note on Mark 16:19.
